title: Microwave shielding of ultracold polar molecules on the transition $\boldsymbol{n=1 \rightarrow 2}$
summary: We show that microwave shielding on the rotational transition $n=1\rightarrow 2$ can be effective in preventing destructive collisions between ultracold polar molecules. It is slightly less efficient than shielding on the transition $0\rightarrow 1$, but has some important advantages. In particular, it does not produce 2-molecule bound states under the conditions needed for shielding, so it will not enhance 3-body recombination. It thus obviates the need for double-field microwave shielding using a second field of different polarization.

AI.tldr: Microwave shielding on the n=1→2 rotational transition effectively prevents destructive collisions between ultracold polar molecules, offering advantages over the 0→1 transition by avoiding 2-molecule bound state formation and eliminating the need for double-field microwave shielding.
AI.motivation: To find an alternative microwave shielding method that prevents destructive collisions between ultracold polar molecules without producing 2-molecule bound states that enhance three-body recombination.
AI.method: The authors investigate microwave shielding on the n=1→2 rotational transition and compare it to the conventional 0→1 transition approach.
AI.result: Shielding on n=1→2 is slightly less efficient than 0→1, but avoids the formation of 2-molecule bound states under shielding conditions, thus not enhancing three-body recombination.
AI.conclusion: Using n=1→2 microwave shielding eliminates the need for complex double-field microwave shielding with different polarization, simplifying experimental implementation for ultracold polar molecule collision control.

title: Complex dynamics in the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick game
comment: 24 pages, 13 figures in the main paper + 2 in appendix
summary: We study the outcome of adaptive learning of a large number of players engaging in sets of two-strategy two-player games. We are interested in typical games, and generate the payoff matrices at random at the beginning. The payoff matrices then remain fixed during the learning process. This provides a game theoretic foundation for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) game, recently introduced by Garnier-Brun, Benzaquen and Bouchaud. The original model by these authors is a special case, with no bias towards any strategy. We here determine stability of learning for SK games with general random bias, and find that the nature of the stable state is affected by random fields. We also introduce a grand-canonical version of the SK game, in which players can choose to abstain. We determine the stability of learning for this game. Our analysis confirms that complex situations involving many players are frequently unlearnable, even if each player only chooses between two different actions. The rate with which players lose memory of past payoffs and the competitiveness of the game emerge as key parameters determining whether learning converges to a unique fixed point, whether there are many fixed points, or if the dynamics remains persistently volatile.

AI.tldr: This paper studies adaptive learning in large populations playing random two-strategy two-player games (SK games), analyzing stability under general random bias and introducing a grand-canonical version with abstention. Key parameters—memory loss rate and competitiveness—determine whether learning converges to a unique fixed point, multiple fixed points, or remains persistently volatile.
AI.motivation: To provide a game-theoretic foundation for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) game and generalize it beyond the unbiased case, understanding how random fields and abstention affect learnability in large games.
AI.method: The authors analytically study the stability of adaptive learning dynamics in SK games with general random bias (random fields) and introduce a grand-canonical version allowing abstention, analyzing the conditions for convergence versus volatility.
AI.result: Stable states are affected by random fields; complex multi-player games are frequently unlearnable even with binary actions. The memory loss rate and competitiveness are key parameters determining three regimes: unique fixed point, multiple fixed points, or persistently volatile dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Learning in large random games often fails to converge, and the nature of the dynamics is governed by the interplay between memory decay and game competitiveness.

title: Fabrication of high-quality topological insulator nanodevices from bulk-insulating air-sensitive Sb-Bi$_2$Se$_3$
comment: 20 pages total; 9 pages main text with 5 figures and 11 pages of supplement with 8 figures
summary: High-quality topological insulator (TI) materials are essential for the realization and detection of Majorana bound states (MBSs) in TI-superconductor hybrid platforms. Widely used compensated TIs exhibit substantial disorder and charge inhomogeneity, which may be detrimental for Majorana devices. In this regard, Sb-substituted Bi$_2$Se$_3$ (SBS) is promising, because it is non-compensated and yet achieves very low bulk carrier density. We systematically investigate the impact of thermal processing during microfabrication on the transport properties of SBS. We developed a room-temperature fabrication protocol that preserves the low carrier density of exfoliated SBS upon fabrication of Hall bar and nanowire devices as evidenced from the observation of quantum interference oscillations in nanowires, a large gate tunability, and clear signatures of weak antilocalization (WAL).

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a room-temperature fabrication protocol for Sb-substituted Bi₂Se₃ (SBS) topological insulator devices that preserves low bulk carrier density, enabling quantum interference oscillations, gate tunability, and weak antilocalization signatures.
AI.motivation: High-quality topological insulator materials are needed for Majorana bound states in TI-superconductor hybrids; widely used compensated TIs suffer from disorder and charge inhomogeneity, motivating the exploration of non-compensated SBS as a promising alternative.
AI.method: Systematic investigation of thermal processing effects during microfabrication on SBS transport properties; developed a room-temperature fabrication protocol for Hall bar and nanowire devices from exfoliated SBS.
AI.result: Room-temperature fabrication preserves low carrier density of exfoliated SBS, evidenced by quantum interference oscillations in nanowires, large gate tunability, and clear weak antilocalization (WAL) signatures.
AI.conclusion: The developed room-temperature fabrication protocol is effective for preserving the intrinsic low carrier density of SBS, making it a suitable material platform for Majorana devices.

title: Enerzyme: A Framework for Efficient Training of Reactive Neural Network Potentials for Enzyme Catalysis with Application to Methyltransferases
summary: Quantum mechanical (QM) cluster models provide an effective framework for mechanistic studies of enzymatic reactions but remain computationally demanding. Neural network potentials (NNPs) offer a promising route to reduce this cost, but enzymes present challenges beyond small molecules, including large system sizes, implicit-solvent environments, substantial polarization, and charge transfer. Here, we present an integrated software framework for efficient NNP training for mechanistic studies of enzymes, demonstrated on QM cluster models of S-adenosyl-L-methionine-dependent methyltransferases (MTases). Our Enerzyme code introduces modular electrostatics-aware NNP architectures and combines automated QM-cluster construction with reactive dataset generation. The Enerzymette subpackage automates reaction pathway exploration at both NNP and DFT levels. We show that iterative flexible scans and nudged elastic band calculations impose stricter requirements on NNPs than conventional dataset metrics. Nevertheless, NNPs trained on fewer than 1,000 system-specific datapoints reproduce reaction energetics and transition-state structures for MTase clusters containing up to 545 atoms with near-chemical accuracy. Direct supervision of atomic charges and consistent dielectric screening substantially improve simulation stability and accuracy, while multitask-learned atomic charges capture charge transfer and polarization trends and provide chemically meaningful descriptors of reactivity. Finally, transferability across chemically diverse catechol O-methyltransferase substrates indicates that NNPs learn generalizable reactivity patterns as training data expand across multiple enzymes. Together, these results establish a foundation for accelerating enzyme mechanistic studies and guide future NNP development for biomolecular reactivity.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Enerzyme, an integrated software framework for training neural network potentials (NNPs) on QM cluster models of enzymes, demonstrating near-chemical accuracy on MTase clusters with up to 545 atoms using fewer than 1,000 datapoints, with enhanced stability via electrostatic-aware architectures and multitask-learned atomic charges.
AI.motivation: QM cluster models are effective for enzymatic mechanistic studies but computationally demanding. NNPs could reduce cost, but enzymes pose challenges including large system sizes, implicit-solvent environments, polarization, and charge transfer that standard NNP methods for small molecules cannot address.
AI.method: Developed Enerzyme code with modular electrostatics-aware NNP architectures, automated QM-cluster construction, reactive dataset generation, and Enerzymette subpackage for automated reaction pathway exploration. Used iterative flexible scans and nudged elastic band calculations; direct supervision of atomic charges and consistent dielectric screening; multitask learning for atomic charges capturing charge transfer and polarization.
AI.result: NNPs trained on fewer than 1,000 system-specific datapoints reproduce reaction energetics and transition-state structures for MTase clusters up to 545 atoms with near-chemical accuracy. Iterative flexible scans and NEB impose stricter requirements than conventional metrics. Direct charge supervision and dielectric screening improve stability and accuracy. Multitask-learned charges capture charge transfer/polarization trends. Transferability across diverse catechol O-methyltransferase substrates shows NNPs learn generalizable reactivity patterns.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a foundation for accelerating enzyme mechanistic studies using NNPs and guides future NNP development for biomolecular reactivity, showing system-specific NNPs can achieve near-chemical accuracy with limited data when properly designed for electrostatic fidelity.

title: Vitriflow: calibrated amorphous structure ensembles from melt-quench simulation
summary: Melt--quench molecular dynamics is widely used to construct amorphous materials models, but the resulting ensemble is defined by choices that are often made implicitly: numerical settings, melt temperature, liquid-hold time, quench rate, system size, and post-generation screening. We introduce vitriflow, a computational materials methodology that turns these choices into an explicit decision chain. The framework couples numerical stability, descriptor-based protocol calibration, user-defined artefact screening, and statistical convergence of the generated analysis ensemble in a material-specific descriptor space. We demonstrate the approach for a-SiO$_2$, a-Si$_3$N$_4$, and a-Sm$_2$O$_3$, which respectively test tetrahedral network fidelity, MG2 $\rightarrow$ PBE $\rightarrow$ HSE06 DFT refinement of a heteropolar nitride, and amorphous/crystal discrimination in a mixed-coordination rare-earth oxide. vitriflow separates defect-free from oxygen-bridge-defective silica, quantifies DFT-refinement response in a common a-Si$_3$N$_4$ structural population, and removes recrystallised Sm$_2$O$_3$ structures without imposing fixed coordination. The result is a reproducible route for generating amorphous ensembles whose numerical settings, thermal protocol, screening actions, and statistical precision are selected from the materials question rather than assumed a priori.

AI.tldr: vitriflow is a methodology that turns implicit choices in melt-quench molecular dynamics into an explicit decision chain, demonstrated for a-SiO₂, a-Si₃N₄, and a-Sm₂O₃ to produce reproducible, material-question-driven amorphous ensembles.
AI.motivation: Melt-quench MD for amorphous materials relies on many implicit choices (e.g., melt temperature, quench rate, system size), leading to poorly defined, irreproducible ensembles. The authors aim to formalize these choices into a transparent, systematic framework.
AI.method: vitriflow couples numerical stability checks, descriptor-based protocol calibration, user-defined artefact screening, and statistical convergence analysis in a material-specific descriptor space. It structures the generation workflow as an explicit decision chain.
AI.result: For a-SiO₂, it separates defect-free from oxygen-bridge-defective structures; for a-Si₃N₄, it quantifies DFT refinement response (MG2→PBE→HSE06) within a common structural population; for a-Sm₂O₃, it removes recrystallised structures without imposing fixed coordination rules.
AI.conclusion: vitriflow provides a reproducible route for generating amorphous ensembles where numerical settings, thermal protocols, screening actions, and statistical precision are selected based on the materials question rather than assumed a priori.

title: Fermiology and spin polarization of topological surface states in PtBi$_2$
summary: Layered PtBi$_2$ is a candidate for topological superconductivity arising in Fermi-arc surface states. Using spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we demonstrate that the Fermi arcs in PtBi$_2$ are singly degenerate and spin-polarized, which establishes their nontrivial topology and constitutes a necessary condition for topological superconductivity. We further uncover a pronounced surface-termination dependence of the Fermi-arc dispersion, yielding either nearly flat or approximately linear bands in agreement with first-principles calculations. Together, the observed spin polarization and termination-dependent bandwidth of the Fermi-arc surface states identify key ingredients underlying the potential emergence of topological superconductivity in PtBi$_2$.

AI.tldr: Using spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, the authors show that Fermi arcs in layered PtBi₂ are singly degenerate and spin-polarized, confirming nontrivial topology. They also find a strong surface-termination dependence of the Fermi-arc dispersion, producing either nearly flat or linear bands. These results highlight key conditions for topological superconductivity in PtBi₂.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether Fermi-arc surface states in PtBi₂ exhibit the necessary properties (spin polarization, nontrivial topology) for topological superconductivity.
AI.method: Spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (spin-ARPES) combined with first-principles calculations.
AI.result: Fermi arcs in PtBi₂ are singly degenerate and spin-polarized, confirming nontrivial topology. The Fermi-arc dispersion strongly depends on surface termination, yielding either nearly flat or approximately linear bands.
AI.conclusion: The observed spin polarization and termination-dependent bandwidth of Fermi-arc surface states identify key ingredients for potential topological superconductivity in PtBi₂.

title: Symmetry and Topology in Wavepacket Dynamics near Conical Intersections
summary: Whether topology directly shapes chemical dynamics remains an open question in theoretical chemistry. The issue arises because degeneracies of adiabatic electronic states can generate nontrivial topological structure, and such degeneracies are common in polyatomic molecules. Existing work has largely emphasized static characterizations and dynamical studies of low-energy, highly symmetric models. Here we develop a symmetry-based analysis of nonadiabatic dynamics in two-state conical-intersection models that is predictive without invoking topological invariants. We show that the nodal-line structures associated with dynamics near a conical intersection are robust in highly symmetric settings, but should not in general be expected to persist once the relevant symmetry is broken.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether topology directly shapes chemical dynamics, focusing on conical intersections in polyatomic molecules. Using symmetry-based analysis of two-state nonadiabatic dynamics, the authors show that nodal-line structures are robust under high symmetry but break down when symmetry is broken, challenging the expectation that topological features persist in general chemical dynamics.
AI.motivation: Whether topology directly shapes chemical dynamics remains an open question in theoretical chemistry, as degeneracies of adiabatic electronic states (common in polyatomic molecules) can generate nontrivial topological structure.
AI.method: Development of a symmetry-based analysis of nonadiabatic dynamics in two-state conical-intersection models that is predictive without invoking topological invariants.
AI.result: Nodal-line structures associated with dynamics near a conical intersection are robust in highly symmetric settings, but should not in general be expected to persist once the relevant symmetry is broken.
AI.conclusion: Topological features in nonadiabatic dynamics are symmetry-protected and not generically robust; symmetry breaking destroys the nodal-line structures traditionally associated with topological effects in chemical dynamics.

title: Verification and Performance Assessment of NuDEAL, a GPU-Accelerated Deterministic Transport Framework on Unstructured Meshes
comment: 39 pages, 14 tables, 15 figures. Author's original manuscript of an article published in Nuclear Science and Engineering. The final published version is available at https://doi.org/10.1080/00295639.2026.2652773
summary: High-fidelity neutronic analyses of advanced reactors require deterministic transport solvers capable of handling complex unstructured geometries while maintaining computational efficiency. This work presents the development and verification of three GPU-accelerated deterministic solvers implemented within a unified framework, Neutronics using Deterministic Finite Element Algorithm (NuDEAL): the planar Method of Characteristics coupled with the Hybrid Finite Element Method (MOC/HFEM), the Discontinuous Galerkin Method of Characteristics (DGMOC), and the Discontinuous Finite Element discrete ordinate method (DFEM-SN). These solvers provide complementary capabilities for consistently solving the multigroup transport equation and can be selectively employed to balance accuracy, computational cost, and memory requirements for a given problem. All methods emphasize efficient GPU execution by leveraging memory alignment, compressed-flux storage, and sequential azimuthal sweeps. The solvers are validated on the C5G7 benchmark and applied to advanced reactor problems, including the ABTR, Empire microreactor, and MSRE. DFEM-SN achieved the highest accuracy, with eigenvalue errors below 50 pcm, while MOC/HFEM and DGMOC provided superior efficiency, with single-GPU runtimes comparable to those of large CPU clusters. The results demonstrate that deterministic GPU solvers on unstructured meshes can deliver both accuracy and scalability, enabling practical whole-core simulations for heterogeneous advanced reactors. The unified NuDEAL framework establishes a foundation for future extensions toward transient and multiphysics analyses on large-scale GPU architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper presents three GPU-accelerated deterministic neutron transport solvers (MOC/HFEM, DGMOC, DFEM-SN) unified under the NuDEAL framework for advanced reactor analysis, demonstrating that DFEM-SN achieves highest accuracy (<50 pcm eigenvalue error) while MOC/HFEM and DGMOC offer superior efficiency on single GPUs comparable to large CPU clusters.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity neutronic analyses of advanced reactors require deterministic transport solvers capable of handling complex unstructured geometries while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.method: Three GPU-accelerated deterministic solvers implemented in the unified NuDEAL framework: planar MOC/HFEM, DGMOC, and DFEM-SN, all leveraging memory alignment, compressed-flux storage, and sequential azimuthal sweeps for efficient GPU execution.
AI.result: DFEM-SN achieved the highest accuracy with eigenvalue errors below 50 pcm; MOC/HFEM and DGMOC provided superior efficiency with single-GPU runtimes comparable to large CPU clusters. Solvers validated on C5G7 benchmark and applied to ABTR, Empire microreactor, and MSRE.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic GPU solvers on unstructured meshes can deliver both accuracy and scalability for practical whole-core simulations of heterogeneous advanced reactors, and the unified NuDEAL framework establishes a foundation for future transient and multiphysics analyses on large-scale GPU architectures.

title: A 2048-spin bulk acoustic wave Ising machine for number partitioning and Sudoku
summary: Optical coherent Ising machines based on time-multiplexing have demonstrated significant progress in terms of connectivity and spin scalability. However, they are constrained by large physical footprints, high power consumption, poor thermal stability, and high cost. Here, we present a time-multiplexed Ising machine leveraging propagating wave packets in solid-state delay lines at microwave frequencies, enabling thermally stable, robust, low-power, tabletop, and affordable design. We use two serially connected 20.5 MHz, 707 μs bulk acoustic wave delay lines supporting 2,048 spins. Our design provides all-to-all connectivity with 15-bit coupling resolution and finds approximate MAX-CUT solutions in 341 ms, potentially scalable to sub-ms by using higher frequency delay lines. Additionally, we demonstrate solutions to number partitioning and Sudoku problems. Compared with state-of-the-art Coherent Ising machines, our machine exhibits four orders of magnitude higher thermal stability. Against the simulated bifurcation algorithm, our design achieves comparable results on the MAX-CUT problem, while outperforming it on the more complex number-partitioning and Sudoku problems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a time-multiplexed Ising machine using microwave-frequency bulk acoustic wave delay lines in solid-state, achieving thermally stable, low-power, tabletop, and affordable operation with 2,048 all-to-all connected spins, solving MAX-CUT, number partitioning, and Sudoku problems with competitive performance.
AI.motivation: Optical coherent Ising machines suffer from large physical footprints, high power consumption, poor thermal stability, and high cost, motivating a more practical alternative.
AI.method: The authors use two serially connected 20.5 MHz, 707 μs bulk acoustic wave delay lines in a time-multiplexed architecture at microwave frequencies, supporting 2,048 spins with all-to-all connectivity and 15-bit coupling resolution.
AI.result: The machine finds approximate MAX-CUT solutions in 341 ms, demonstrates four orders of magnitude higher thermal stability than state-of-the-art Coherent Ising machines, and achieves comparable MAX-CUT results while outperforming simulated bifurcation on number partitioning and Sudoku problems.
AI.conclusion: Solid-state microwave delay-line-based Ising machines offer a thermally stable, low-power, and cost-effective alternative to optical CIMs, with potential for sub-ms scalability using higher frequency delay lines.

title: Microscopic origins of inertial magnetization dynamics
comment: Main text: 4 pages 2 figures. Supplementary text: 9 pages 3 figures
summary: Ultrafast experiments have uncovered inertial magnetization dynamics in ferromagnets, but their microscopic origin remains elusive. Using a non-Markovian quantum master equation we show that inertial dynamics arise from coherent interactions with optical phonons in the lattice. The fast optical frequency explains the nutation observed on picosecond timescales and accounts for variations between experiments through substrate-dependent phonon damping. By establishing magnon{phonon coupling as the microscopic basis of inertial magnetization, our results open new pathways for tailoring ultrafast spin dynamics and controlling magnetic states at terahertz frequencies.

AI.tldr: The paper explains that inertial magnetization dynamics in ferromagnets, observed in ultrafast experiments, originate from coherent magnon-phonon coupling with optical lattice phonons, modeled via a non-Markovian quantum master equation. This mechanism accounts for picosecond nutation timescales and substrate-dependent variations, opening routes for terahertz spin control.
AI.motivation: To uncover the microscopic origin of inertial magnetization dynamics in ferromagnets observed in ultrafast experiments, which has remained elusive despite experimental evidence.
AI.method: Non-Markovian quantum master equation to model coherent interactions between magnons and optical phonons in the lattice.
AI.result: Inertial dynamics arise from coherent magnon-phonon coupling; the optical phonon frequency explains picosecond nutation timescales; substrate-dependent phonon damping accounts for experimental variations.
AI.conclusion: Magnon-phonon coupling is established as the microscopic basis of inertial magnetization, enabling tailored ultrafast spin dynamics and terahertz-frequency magnetic state control.

title: Electrical transport in ultra-thin films: from Fuchs-Sondheimer to quantum-confinement
summary: Ultra-thin films are fundamental components of modern nanoelectronics, where reducing thickness to the few-nanometer scale leads to a dramatic increase in electrical resistivity. For decades, this behavior has been interpreted in terms of classical size effects, primarily surface scattering within the Fuchs--Sondheimer theory and grain-boundary scattering in the Mayadas--Shatzkes model. While these approaches successfully describe transport when the film thickness is comparable to the electronic mean free path, growing experimental evidence indicates that they become insufficient under extreme confinement. This review discusses the crossover from classical scattering to a quantum-confinement regime in which the electronic states available for transport are fundamentally restructured by finite size. We review the recently proposed reciprocal-space confinement theory, which predicts an exponential increase of resistivity with decreasing thickness at the nanoscale, and discuss how it can be combined with classical surface-scattering models to provide a unified description of ultra-thin metallic and semiconducting films. Finally, we summarize recent experimental evidence supporting this picture and discuss its implications for future nanoelectronic devices, nanoscale interconnects, and quantum transport under extreme spatial confinement.

AI.tldr: This review examines the transition from classical size effects (Fuchs-Sondheimer and Mayadas-Shatzkes models) to quantum-confinement regimes in ultra-thin films, presenting a reciprocal-space confinement theory that predicts exponential resistivity increase at the nanoscale, and proposes a unified framework combining quantum and classical scattering for metallic and semiconducting films.
AI.motivation: Classical scattering models (Fuchs-Sondheimer and Mayadas-Shatzkes) fail to describe electrical resistivity under extreme confinement (few-nanometer thickness), motivating the need for a unified theory incorporating quantum-confinement effects.
AI.method: The paper reviews reciprocal-space confinement theory, which predicts an exponential increase of resistivity with decreasing thickness at the nanoscale, and proposes combining it with classical surface-scattering models for a unified description.
AI.result: The reciprocal-space confinement theory successfully describes the exponential resistivity increase in ultra-thin films beyond classical predictions, and can be integrated with existing classical models.
AI.conclusion: The unified framework combining quantum confinement and classical scattering provides a complete description of transport in ultra-thin metallic and semiconducting films, with implications for nanoelectronic devices, interconnects, and quantum transport under extreme spatial confinement.

title: Disorder-induced superconductivity in graphene
summary: Correlated phases of matter are typically investigated in crystalline systems, where disorder is considered to be detrimental. However, intriguing exceptions exist, such as superconductivity being enhanced in amorphous realizations of Al and Bi. Here, we demonstrate that superconductivity can even emerge entirely from disorder, using monolayer graphene as an example. In the clean limit, the semi-metallic nature of graphene requires prohibitively strong electronic interactions to achieve superconductivity. Despite the inherently random nature of disorder, we show that introducing low concentrations of vacancies or hydrogenation in graphene provides a large density of low-energy states that easily induce superconductivity. For conventional $s$-wave pairing, disorder induces a finite superconducting order parameter for arbitrarily weak attractive interactions. Rather than forming isolated superconducting puddles, global phase coherence is established through a finite superfluid weight of purely geometrical origin. Away from the chiral limit of vacancies, hydrogenation similarly yields a finite transition temperature and nonzero superfluid weight for weak interactions. For unconventional nearest-neighbor pairing, typically more disrupted by disorder, superconductivity exhibits quantum-critical-like behavior, yet phase coherence persists at low interaction strengths, with mixed $d$-wave symmetries. Our work demonstrates the robust emergence of macroscopic superconducting phase coherence engineered entirely from microscopic disorder.

AI.tldr: Superconductivity can emerge entirely from disorder in monolayer graphene, where introducing vacancies or hydrogenation creates low-energy states that induce global superconducting coherence even for arbitrarily weak attractive interactions, demonstrating disorder-engineered macroscopic phase coherence.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that superconductivity can emerge entirely from disorder in a system (monolayer graphene) where clean-limit superconductivity is prohibitively difficult, challenging the conventional view that disorder is always detrimental to correlated phases.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of monolayer graphene with introduced disorder (vacancies or hydrogenation) using a framework that examines s-wave and unconventional nearest-neighbor pairing, calculating superconducting order parameters, transition temperatures, superfluid weight, and phase coherence properties.
AI.result: Disorder induces a finite superconducting order parameter for arbitrarily weak attractive s-wave interactions; global phase coherence is established via superfluid weight of purely geometric origin; hydrogenation similarly yields finite Tc and superfluid weight; unconventional pairing exhibits quantum-critical-like behavior with mixed d-wave symmetries.
AI.conclusion: Macroscopic superconducting phase coherence can be robustly engineered entirely from microscopic disorder, establishing disorder as a viable route to induce superconductivity in systems where it would not otherwise occur.

title: First passage time distribution in underdamped harmonic oscillators
summary: We derive the distribution of the first passage time $t_{fp}$ for the position $x$ of an underdamped harmonic oscillator to overcome a threshold $x_B$. As the $t_{fp}$ distribution depends on the oscillator quality factor $Q$ different approaches are used. At very large quality factor ($Q\gg 100$) and intermediate and long $t_{fp}$ the proof is based on an energy diffusion model, whereas at medium quality factor ($Q\sim 10$) the proof is based on the study of the eigenvalues of the Kramers linear differential operator with absorbing boundary conditions. For all $Q$ and short $t_{fp}$ we use a Hamiltonian approximation. The theoretical predictions are in excellent agreement with direct numerical simulations of underdamped oscillator dynamics. Finally we show that the mean of the trajectories ending at $t_{fp}$ presents a particular shape driven by a specific noise pattern.

AI.tldr: This paper derives the first passage time distribution for an underdamped harmonic oscillator crossing a threshold, using different analytical approaches depending on the quality factor Q, and validates them with numerical simulations.
AI.motivation: To derive the distribution of the first passage time for an underdamped harmonic oscillator crossing a threshold, which depends on the oscillator quality factor Q.
AI.method: For very large Q (≫100) and intermediate/long times: energy diffusion model. For medium Q (~10): eigenvalue analysis of the Kramers linear differential operator with absorbing boundary conditions. For all Q and short times: Hamiltonian approximation.
AI.result: Theoretical predictions show excellent agreement with direct numerical simulations of underdamped oscillator dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The mean trajectory shape at the first passage time is driven by a specific noise pattern.

title: Generalized quantum geometry formulated through interacting vertex correlations
summary: Quantum geometry characterizes the variation of electron wavefunctions in solids along a parameter space. Conventionally, crystal momentum is chosen as the parameter, since it couples to electromagnetic fields, offering an interpretation of quantum geometry in terms of dipole matrix elements, polarization fluctuations, and optical responses. However, Bloch momentum is not the only possible parameter space in which a wavefunction can evolve. In this work, we show that quantum geometry can be extended beyond the bare Bloch-band geometry to manifolds whose adiabatic parameters represent deformations of the ground state, including collective bosonic fluctuations, external fields, or structural distortions. We show that the generalized quantum geometric tensor is encoded by correlations of interacting vertices, conjugate to the deformation parameters. By way of illustration, we briefly discuss the application of these extended geometric concepts to manifolds generated by Hubbard-Stratonovich bosonic fields, or Jahn-Teller configurational spaces. The formulation presented here is framed by general manifolds, which extend quantum geometry to generic structural, collective, and interactive many-body systems.

AI.tldr: The paper extends quantum geometry beyond conventional Bloch-band manifolds to generalized parameter spaces representing deformations of ground states, including collective bosonic fluctuations, external fields, or structural distortions, with the generalized quantum geometric tensor encoded by correlations of interacting vertices.
AI.motivation: To generalize quantum geometry beyond the conventional Bloch momentum parameter space, enabling its application to broader many-body systems where wavefunctions evolve under deformations such as collective fluctuations, external fields, or structural distortions.
AI.method: The authors extend the quantum geometric tensor formalism to general manifolds where adiabatic parameters represent ground-state deformations, showing that the generalized geometric tensor is encoded by correlations of vertices conjugate to deformation parameters.
AI.result: A generalized quantum geometric tensor framework applicable to manifolds generated by Hubbard-Stratonovich bosonic fields, Jahn-Teller configurational spaces, and other many-body systems.
AI.conclusion: Quantum geometry can be extended to generic structural, collective, and interacting many-body systems beyond the conventional Bloch-band setting.

title: Quantum Heat Under the Microscope: A Perspective on Cryogenic Scanning Thermal Microscopy
summary: Exploring thermal transport at cryogenic temperatures presents both significant challenges and valuable insights. By uncovering the thermal counterpart of well-known quantum phenomena, researchers investigated fascinating phenomena ranging from the violation of the Wiedemann-Franz law to the quantisation of phonons. One key frontier remains : no existing method can image local heat transport at the nanoscale under cryogenic conditions. In this Perspective, we review the current state state of the art of local heat transport characterisation techniques and highlight their limitations. As a motivation for the development of cryogenic Scanning Thermal Microscopy, we provide five case studies illustrating how this approach could deepen our understanding of exotic quantum phases and enable the emergence of transformative technologies.

AI.tldr: This Perspective reviews the limitations of current local heat transport characterization techniques at cryogenic temperatures and motivates the development of cryogenic Scanning Thermal Microscopy through five case studies, aiming to deepen understanding of exotic quantum phases and enable transformative technologies.
AI.motivation: No existing method can image local heat transport at the nanoscale under cryogenic conditions, limiting the understanding of quantum phenomena such as Wiedemann-Franz law violation and phonon quantization.
AI.method: The authors review the current state-of-the-art local heat transport characterization techniques, identify their limitations, and propose cryogenic Scanning Thermal Microscopy as a solution, supported by five case studies.
AI.result: Five case studies demonstrate how cryogenic Scanning Thermal Microscopy could potentially deepen the understanding of exotic quantum phases and enable transformative technologies.
AI.conclusion: Developing cryogenic Scanning Thermal Microscopy is essential to overcome existing limitations and unlock new insights into quantum heat transport phenomena and related technologies.

title: Benchmarking SOPPA-based methods for the calculation of static and dynamic polarizabilities
summary: Static and frequency-dependent polarizabilities were computed for 41 molecules using RPA, RPA(D), HRPA, HRPA(D), SOPPA, SOPPA(CC2), and SOPPA(CCSD) with the aug-cc-pVTZ basis set and benchmarked against CCSD reference values and available experimental data. The analysis reveals a pronounced distinction between the performance of these methods for aromatic versus non-aromatic molecules. Across all frequencies, HRPA consistently yields substantially larger deviations from CCSD than the other approaches, whereas HRPA(D) and SOPPA(CCSD) provide the most accurate results overall. For static polarizabilities, HRPA(D) performs best for non-aromatic systems, followed by SOPPA(CCSD) and RPA(D), while SOPPA(CCSD) is most accurate for aromatic molecules. In the frequency-dependent regime, HRPA(D) remains the most accurate method for non-aromatic molecules, although RPA(D) shows greater consistency. For aromatic molecules, SOPPA(CCSD) performs best at low frequencies, with RPA offering intermediate accuracy but higher consistency than most other methods; at higher frequencies, RPA becomes the most accurate approach, followed by RPA(D), while SOPPA(CCSD) deteriorates. These trends highlight the importance of doubles corrections in RPA(D) and HRPA(D), which achieve accuracy comparable to or better than SOPPA(CCSD) at lower computational cost. The strong performance of RPA for aromatic molecules is attributed to its characteristic overestimation of the lowest electronic excitation energy. Comparison with experimental data confirms SOPPA(CCSD) as the most reliable method for static polarizabilities, while RPA and HRPA(D) provide the best agreement for frequency-dependent polarizabilities of aromatic systems.

AI.tldr: The study benchmarks various computational methods (RPA, RPA(D), HRPA, HRPA(D), SOPPA, SOPPA(CC2), SOPPA(CCSD)) for computing static and frequency-dependent polarizabilities of 41 molecules, finding that HRPA(D) and SOPPA(CCSD) are most accurate overall, with notable performance differences between aromatic and non-aromatic systems.
AI.motivation: To systematically evaluate and compare the accuracy of multiple computational methods (RPA-based and SOPPA variants) for predicting static and frequency-dependent polarizabilities, particularly examining performance differences between aromatic and non-aromatic molecules.
AI.method: Computed static and frequency-dependent polarizabilities for 41 molecules using RPA, RPA(D), HRPA, HRPA(D), SOPPA, SOPPA(CC2), and SOPPA(CCSD) with aug-cc-pVTZ basis set, benchmarked against CCSD reference values and experimental data.
AI.result: HRPA(D) and SOPPA(CCSD) provide the most accurate results overall. HRPA(D) excels for non-aromatic systems; SOPPA(CCSD) is best for aromatic molecules. RPA performs well for aromatic molecules at higher frequencies due to overestimation of lowest excitation energy. Doubles corrections (RPA(D), HRPA(D)) achieve accuracy comparable to SOPPA(CCSD) at lower cost.
AI.conclusion: SOPPA(CCSD) is most reliable for static polarizabilities; RPA and HRPA(D) yield best agreement for frequency-dependent polarizabilities of aromatic systems. The choice of optimal method depends on molecular type (aromatic vs. non-aromatic) and frequency regime.

title: Predicting Novel Stable Materials for Experimental Synthesis
summary: Machine-learning-accelerated materials discovery has yielded large numbers of computationally stable compounds, yet many remain experimentally unrealized, underscoring a persistent gap between prediction and synthesis. Here, we introduce a hierarchical screening framework that combines PBE-based thermodynamic stability, efficient dynamical-stability screening enabled by universal machine-learning interatomic potentials, and SCAN-based thermodynamic refinement. Applying this protocol to the 894 stable materials previously reported in Sci. Data 9, 302 (2022), we first curate 603 unique structures, of which only 298 remain thermodynamically stable on the complete PBE phase diagrams, demonstrating the critical role of competing phases in stability assessment. Dynamical screening then identifies 166 materials stable under both harmonic-phonon and finite-temperature molecular dynamics criteria, and SCAN phase diagrams further narrow this set to 109. Finally, by combining decomposition enthalpy with chemical-space completeness, we prioritize 25 candidates as high-confidence targets for experimental synthesis. This work provides a practical protocol for translating stability predictions into experimentally actionable synthesis targets, closing a key gap in machine-learning-driven materials discovery.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical screening framework combining PBE thermodynamics, machine-learning phonon stability, and SCAN refinement reduces 894 predicted stable materials to 25 high-confidence experimental synthesis targets, closing the prediction-to-synthesis gap.
AI.motivation: Machine-learning-accelerated materials discovery produces many computationally stable compounds that remain experimentally unrealized, highlighting a persistent gap between computational prediction and experimental synthesis.
AI.method: A three-stage hierarchical screening: (1) PBE-based thermodynamic stability assessment with competing phases, (2) dynamical stability screening via universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (harmonic phonon + finite-temperature MD), (3) SCAN-based thermodynamic refinement, followed by decomposition enthalpy and chemical-space completeness prioritization.
AI.result: From 894 stable materials, 603 unique structures were curated; 298 remained thermodynamically stable on PBE phase diagrams; 166 passed dynamical screening; 109 survived SCAN phase diagrams; 25 were prioritized as high-confidence synthesis targets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed protocol provides a practical pathway to translate computational stability predictions into experimentally actionable synthesis targets, effectively bridging the gap in machine-learning-driven materials discovery.

title: Differentiable inverse design of short-range order in high-entropy alloys: from target sro to target property
summary: Short-range order (SRO) governs the mechanical response of multi-principal-element alloys, but designing an alloy for a target property usually means solving two disconnected problems: building a structure matching a desired SRO pattern, then separately checking its property, with no shared optimization. This work replaces the standard random-swap search (reverse Monte Carlo) with a gradient-based approach: atom occupancy is treated as continuous rather than fixed, so the whole process can be tuned using gradient descent, the same method used to train neural networks. This builder matches random-swap accuracy on small systems, but is six times faster and eight times more accurate on large 4000-atom systems, and scales smoothly to alloys with many elements without extra bookkeeping. A physics-based correction term, adapted from prior two-element work and extended here to many elements, keeps designed structures thermodynamically realistic rather than just numerically matching the target SRO pattern. A small neural network then predicts mechanical properties directly from composition and SRO statistics, closing the loop from target property back to structure. Tested on nine face-centered-cubic and body-centered-cubic alloys, the pipeline captured SRO-driven stiffness changes from -20% to +57%, and cell-size checks showed at least 864 atoms are needed to get the direction and size of these changes right, since the commonly used 108-atom cells can mislead. Against real simulations for a cobalt-chromium-nickel alloy, the method matched three of four target stiffness values within 6%. The method is released as an open-source Python package, anisro, offering a practical route to gradient-based, property-driven alloy design.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a gradient-based (rather than random-swap) method for designing multi-principal-element alloys with desired short-range order (SRO), achieving faster and more accurate structure generation, and closes the design loop by using a neural network to predict mechanical properties from SRO statistics so properties guide structure optimization.
AI.motivation: Current alloy design for target properties suffers from a disconnect: building a structure matching a desired SRO pattern and checking its property are separate, unoptimized steps. This work aims to unify them into a single gradient-based pipeline.
AI.method: Replaces standard random-swap reverse Monte Carlo with a gradient-based approach where atom occupancy is treated as continuous, enabling gradient descent optimization. A physics-based correction term (extended from two-element to many-element alloys) ensures thermodynamic realism. A small neural network predicts mechanical properties from composition and SRO statistics.
AI.result: Matches random-swap accuracy on small systems; six times faster and eight times more accurate on 4000-atom systems. Captured SRO-driven stiffness changes from -20% to +57% across nine FCC/BCC alloys. Showed at least 864 atoms needed (108-atom cells mislead). Matched three of four target stiffness values within 6% for a Co-Cr-Ni alloy.
AI.conclusion: The method, released as the open-source Python package anisro, provides a practical route to gradient-based, property-driven alloy design, closing the loop from target property back to structure.

title: Ultrasonic Observation of Slowing Down of Multipole Fluctuations in Sr$_2$RuO$_4$
summary: We performed ultrasonic measurements on the unconventional superconductor Sr$_2$RuO$_4$ to investigate the dynamical properties of the electronic states near its superconducting transition temperature, $T_\mathrm{c} = 1.4$ K. We observed an increase in the in-plane transverse ultrasonic attenuation coefficient as the temperature approached $T_\mathrm{c}$. The ultrasonic attenuation exhibited a Landau-Khalatnikov-type ultrasonic frequency dependence with a typical relaxation time of approximately $10^{-10}$ s. Under an applied magnetic field of 10 T, the superconducting transition was suppressed. However, the ultrasonic attenuation coefficient exhibited an increase down to low temperatures, indicating the slowing down of fluctuations associated with multipole degrees of freedom. Based on group-theoretical considerations, we propose that the electric hexadecapole plays a crucial role in the slowing down. Furthermore, we discuss the relationship between multi-component superconducting order parameters and multipole degrees of freedom.

AI.tldr: Ultrasonic measurements on Sr₂RuO₄ reveal a Landau-Khalatnikov-type attenuation increase near Tc (~1.4 K) with ~10⁻¹⁰ s relaxation time, attributed to electric hexadecapole fluctuations, linking multipole degrees of freedom to multi-component superconducting order parameters.
AI.motivation: To investigate the dynamical properties of electronic states near the superconducting transition temperature of Sr₂RuO₄, particularly the role of multipole degrees of freedom in unconventional superconductivity.
AI.method: In-plane transverse ultrasonic attenuation measurements on Sr₂RuO₄ near Tc = 1.4 K, with frequency-dependent analysis (Landau-Khalatnikov type) and magnetic field suppression (10 T), combined with group-theoretical considerations.
AI.result: Observed increase in ultrasonic attenuation coefficient near Tc with ~10⁻¹⁰ s relaxation time; under 10 T field, attenuation still increased down to low temperatures, indicating slowing down of multipole fluctuations.
AI.conclusion: Electric hexadecapole fluctuations are responsible for the observed ultrasonic attenuation anomaly, and multi-component superconducting order parameters are linked to multipole degrees of freedom.

title: Sandpile Models on complex networks
summary: We investigate the sandpile model on complex networks by developing a branching-process framework that explicitly incorporates dissipation during avalanche propagation. Unlike classical branching descriptions, which assume conservative transport and locally tree-like independence, the present approach introduces grain-loss effects directly into the offspring distribution, yielding generalized generating functions for dissipative avalanche dynamics. In the dissipative regime, avalanche-size distributions acquire exponential cutoffs while preserving topology-dependent scaling behavior. Numerical simulations confirm the theoretical predictions on sparse random networks and reveal systematic deviations in highly structured topologies. In particular, by using Holme-Kim clustered scale-free networks, we show that increasing clustering continuously lowers the avalanche exponent and enhances the probability of large cascades, demonstrating that short cycles generate strong correlations that invalidate the classical independent-branch approx imation. Surprisingly, trees also exhibit substantial deviations from power-law because low edge density and the abundance of leaves constrain avalanche propagation. These results show that dissipation, clustering, and sparse connectivity fundamentally reshape avalanche size distribution of the sandpile model on networks and establish quantitative limits for branching-process descriptions of avalanche dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the branching-process framework for the sandpile model on complex networks by incorporating dissipation, showing that avalanche-size distributions develop exponential cutoffs while retaining topology-dependent scaling. Simulations reveal that clustering in Holme-Kim networks lowers the avalanche exponent and increases large cascades, while trees deviate from power-law behavior due to sparse connectivity.
AI.motivation: Classical branching-process descriptions of the sandpile model assume conservative transport and locally tree-like independence, neglecting dissipation and topological correlations. The authors aim to develop a generalized framework that explicitly incorporates grain-loss effects to better understand how dissipation, clustering, and sparse connectivity reshape avalanche dynamics on complex networks.
AI.method: A branching-process framework is developed where dissipation effects are incorporated directly into the offspring distribution, yielding generalized generating functions for dissipative avalanche dynamics. Numerical simulations are performed on sparse random networks and Holme-Kim clustered scale-free networks to validate theoretical predictions and examine the role of clustering and sparse connectivity.
AI.result: Avalanche-size distributions exhibit exponential cutoffs in the dissipative regime while preserving topology-dependent scaling. Clustering in Holme-Kim networks continuously lowers the avalanche exponent and increases the probability of large cascades. Trees deviate from power-law behavior due to low edge density and abundance of leaves constraining propagation. Systematic deviations from classical branching approximations are observed in highly structured topologies.
AI.conclusion: Dissipation, clustering, and sparse connectivity fundamentally reshape avalanche size distributions in the sandpile model on networks. Short cycles generate strong correlations that invalidate the classical independent-branch approximation, establishing quantitative limits for branching-process descriptions of avalanche dynamics.

title: Nonperturbative Nonlinear Hall Effect in Nonequilibrium Steady States
summary: The nonlinear Hall effect in quantum materials has attracted broad interest, yet most existing studies focus on the weak-field, perturbative regime. Here we develop a nonperturbative approach based on nonequilibrium steady-state Green's functions for dc-field-driven lattice systems, with dissipation and interactions incorporated through self-energies beyond the constant relaxation-time approximation and interband transitions treated alongside their intraband counterparts. Applied to a two-band semimetal model, our approach provides direct access to the strong-field Hall response beyond the nonperturbative crossover where the edge of the nonequilibrium distribution reaches Berry-curvature hot spots, a regime in which constant relaxation-time estimates and Berry curvature dipole calculations become unreliable. We further demonstrate that interaction and electron-phonon self-energies within dynamical mean-field theory can substantially change the Hall signal. Our framework enables quantitative simulations of nonequilibrium nonlinear Hall phenomena and provides guidance for strong-field transport experiments.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a nonperturbative approach using nonequilibrium steady-state Green's functions to study the nonlinear Hall effect in quantum materials under strong DC fields, going beyond the weak-field perturbative regime where constant relaxation-time and Berry curvature dipole approximations fail. Applied to a two-band semimetal, their method captures strong-field Hall response and shows that interaction/electron-phonon self-energies via DMFT can significantly alter the Hall signal.
AI.motivation: Existing studies of the nonlinear Hall effect focus on the weak-field, perturbative regime, leaving the strong-field nonperturbative regime unexplored and lacking reliable theoretical tools.
AI.method: They develop a nonperturbative approach based on nonequilibrium steady-state Green's functions for dc-field-driven lattice systems, incorporating dissipation and interactions through self-energies beyond the constant relaxation-time approximation, and treating interband and intraband transitions on equal footing.
AI.result: Applied to a two-band semimetal, the approach captures the strong-field Hall response beyond the nonperturbative crossover where Berry-curvature hot spots are reached; constant relaxation-time and Berry curvature dipole estimates become unreliable in this regime. Interaction and electron-phonon self-energies within DMFT substantially change the Hall signal.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables quantitative simulations of nonequilibrium nonlinear Hall phenomena and provides guidance for strong-field transport experiments.

title: An efficient formalism for inertial spin waves: Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya antiferromagnets as case studies
summary: Magnetic inertia, emerging in the ultrafast regime, supports inertial spin waves (SWs) as novel magnetic excitations. Despite considerable efforts devoted to inertial SWs, a systematic formalism for fully characterizing their intrinsic properties, especially chirality and polarization, is still lacking, and inertial SWs in spatially nonuniform magnetic configurations remain poorly explored. Here, we develop a framework for calculating inertial SWs and establish a general definition of their chirality and polarization via the ellipticity angle, a unified parameter encoding frequency sign, phase difference, and elliptical axis ratio. Using this method, we systematically investigate precessional and nutational SWs in uniaxial antiferromagnets with staggered and homogeneous Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions (DMIs), covering uniform collinear, canted, and spiral magnetic configurations. The results reveal that small staggered DMI preserves spin-wave degeneracy, whereas small homogeneous DMI lifts it. Further space-time inversion symmetry breaking in canted and spiral structures fully removes spin-wave degeneracy across the entire Brillouin zone. Long-wavelength nutational SWs behave as backward waves, and flat bands emerge in canted and spiral configurations near a critical inertial relaxation time. In canted and spiral configurations, nutational modes are always lefthanded whereas precessional modes are always righthanded; additionally, the dispersion spectra of the canted configuration can be derived from those of the spiral configuration via band folding. Polarization is wavenumber insensitive for uniform configurations but becomes strongly dispersive for nonuniform ones. This work advances the fundamental understanding of magnetic inertial dynamics and provides theoretical insights for the development of ultrafast magnonic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a framework for calculating inertial spin waves (SWs) in antiferromagnets, defining chirality and polarization via ellipticity angle. It systematically studies precessional and nutational SWs in uniaxial antiferromagnets with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions across collinear, canted, and spiral configurations, revealing degeneracy breaking, backward wave behavior, and polarization characteristics.
AI.motivation: Despite progress on inertial SWs, a systematic formalism for characterizing their intrinsic properties (chirality, polarization) is lacking, and inertial SWs in spatially nonuniform magnetic configurations remain poorly explored.
AI.method: A framework for calculating inertial SWs is developed, using ellipticity angle to define chirality and polarization. The method is applied to uniaxial antiferromagnets with staggered/homogeneous DMIs, covering uniform collinear, canted, and spiral configurations.
AI.result: Small staggered DMI preserves SW degeneracy; small homogeneous DMI lifts it. Space-time inversion symmetry breaking in canted/spiral structures fully removes degeneracy. Long-wavelength nutational SWs are backward waves; flat bands emerge near critical inertial relaxation time. Nutational modes are left-handed, precessional modes right-handed in nonuniform configurations. Dispersion of canted case derives from spiral via band folding. Polarization is wavenumber-insensitive for uniform but strongly dispersive for nonuniform configurations.
AI.conclusion: This work advances fundamental understanding of magnetic inertial dynamics and provides theoretical insights for ultrafast magnonic devices.

title: On the Symplectic Propagation of the Spin-MInt Algorithm for Non-Adiabatic Quantum Dynamics
comment: 45 pages, 2 figures, submitted to Journal of Mathematical Chemistry
summary: Mapping methods are often used for the numerical simulation of nonadiabatic systems by propagating classical mapping variable trajectories. A recently popularised mapping method is spin-mapping, whose mapping variables arise from quantum mechanical operators with symmetries described by a Lie-Poisson algebra. Simulating the classical-like dynamics of spin-mapping systems accurately is generally challenging, with many methods unable to preserve the underlying geometric structure of the symplectic form. The Spin-MInt algorithm is a recently proposed algorithm propagating spin-mapping variables, with a direct proof of symplecticity existing only for 2 electronic states. Here, we directly prove the symplecticity of the Spin-MInt algorithm for a general $K$ electronic states. A review of the symplectic nature of coadjoint orbits of the $\mathfrak{su}(K)$ Lie-Poisson algebra provides the framework needed to understand symplecticity of the Spin-MInt algorithm in this general case. The symplecticity of the method on the associated coadjoint orbit is then shown for what we believe to be the first time via an explicit verification of the symplecticity condition $\mathbf{MJ}\mathbf{M}^\textrm{T}=\mathbf{J}$ exploiting the Lie-Poisson structure of the system. To our knowledge, this is the first time the monodromy matrix for the Spin-MInt algorithm has been explicitly stated using canonical coordinates on the coherent state manifold for a general number of states. We hope that this will assist the development of classical-like spin-mapping methods which might utilise elements of the monodromy matrix, and inform future work on similar symplectic algorithms for coupled and uncoupled Lie-Poisson systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proves the symplecticity of the Spin-MInt algorithm for a general K electronic states, extending the prior proof limited to 2 states, by leveraging the Lie-Poisson structure of $\mathfrak{su}(K)$ coadjoint orbits and explicitly verifying the symplecticity condition $\mathbf{MJ}\mathbf{M}^\textrm{T}=\mathbf{J}$.
AI.motivation: Prior proof of symplecticity for the Spin-MInt algorithm existed only for 2 electronic states; a general proof for K states was needed to validate the geometric structure preservation of the method for arbitrary multi-state nonadiabatic dynamics simulations.
AI.method: The authors provide a direct proof of symplecticity by reviewing the symplectic nature of coadjoint orbits of the $\mathfrak{su}(K)$ Lie-Poisson algebra, formulating the monodromy matrix in canonical coordinates on the coherent state manifold for general K, and explicitly verifying the symplecticity condition $\mathbf{MJ}\mathbf{M}^\textrm{T}=\mathbf{J}$.
AI.result: First explicit verification that the Spin-MInt algorithm is symplectic for a general number K of electronic states, with the monodromy matrix stated in canonical coordinates on the coherent state manifold for the first time.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes the symplectic nature of Spin-MInt for general K states, which may assist development of classical-like spin-mapping methods and inform future symplectic algorithms for coupled/uncoupled Lie-Poisson systems.

title: Efficient Large-Scale STEM-EELS Simulations With Torched-TACAW
summary: The time auto-correlation of auxiliary wave functions (TACAW) method enables efficient simulations of ultra-low-loss electron energy loss spectra (EELS) arising from vibrational and magnon excitations. In practical applications to realistic materials systems, however, TACAW calculations become challenging due to the large system sizes required for models containing defects, interfaces, impurities, or grain boundaries, as well as the substantial computational cost and data throughput associated with molecular dynamics and multislice calculations. Here we discuss a practical methodology for large-scale TACAW simulations and present torched-TACAW, a freely available implementation of the TACAW part of the described workflow for efficient STEM-EELS simulations. The overall approach combines molecular dynamics based on foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials, partitioning of elongated supercells, and on-the-fly processing of multislice outputs in order to enable near ab initio quality simulations with tractable memory use and data flow. Using rutile TiO2 as a model system, we analyze important numerical aspects of the method, including windowing and supercell partitioning, and demonstrate atomic-resolution STEM-EELS simulations for thick samples.

AI.tldr: The paper presents torched-TACAW, a practical implementation of the TACAW method for efficient, large-scale STEM-EELS simulations combining machine-learned interatomic potentials, supercell partitioning, and on-the-fly multislice processing to achieve near ab initio quality with manageable memory and data throughput.
AI.motivation: TACAW calculations for ultra-low-loss EELS simulations become challenging for realistic materials systems (defects, interfaces, impurities, grain boundaries) due to large required system sizes and high computational cost/data throughput of molecular dynamics and multislice calculations.
AI.method: The methodology combines (1) molecular dynamics using foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials, (2) partitioning of elongated supercells, and (3) on-the-fly processing of multislice outputs. This is implemented in a freely available code called torched-TACAW.
AI.result: Using rutile TiO2 as a model system, numerical aspects such as windowing and supercell partitioning were analyzed. Atomic-resolution STEM-EELS simulations for thick samples were demonstrated with near ab initio quality while maintaining tractable memory use and data flow.
AI.conclusion: torched-TACAW enables practical large-scale TACAW simulations for ultra-low-loss EELS, overcoming prior computational limitations through efficient partitioning and on-the-fly processing strategies.

title: Phase-selective orbital-charge conversion in $\mathrm{MoTe_2}$
summary: Two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have emerged as promising materials for spin--orbitronics owing to their strong spin--orbit coupling and rich electronic phases. However, their orbital transport properties remain largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that the orbitronic response of $\mathrm{MoTe_2}$ is governed by a thickness-driven structural phase transition. RF-sputtered $\mathrm{MoTe_2}$ thin films exhibit a crossover at a critical thickness of approximately $4.5\,\mathrm{nm}$, stabilizing in the metallic $1T^\prime$ phase below this threshold and in the semiconducting $2H$ phase above it. Raman spectroscopy and scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS) confirm the structural and electronic transition, revealing gapless behavior in ultrathin films and a finite band gap in thicker samples. Spin-pumping measurements detect an additional transverse charge-conversion signal exclusively in metallic $1T^\prime$-$\mathrm{MoTe_2}$, in agreement with first-principles calculations that identify a dominant orbital Rashba--Edelstein response as the underlying conversion mechanism.

AI.tldr: MoTe₂ thin films undergo a thickness-driven structural phase transition (1T′ metallic below ~4.5 nm, 2H semiconducting above), enabling a dominant orbital Rashba–Edelstein conversion mechanism detected via spin-pumping measurements exclusively in the 1T′ phase.
AI.motivation: To explore the largely unexplored orbital transport properties of two-dimensional TMDs and understand how structural phases influence orbitronic responses.
AI.method: RF-sputtered MoTe₂ thin films of varying thicknesses; characterization by Raman spectroscopy and scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS); spin-pumping measurements; first-principles calculations to identify the conversion mechanism.
AI.result: A critical thickness of ~4.5 nm separates metallic 1T′ (gapless, ultrathin) from semiconducting 2H (finite bandgap, thicker) phases. Only metallic 1T′-MoTe₂ exhibits an additional transverse charge-conversion signal in spin-pumping experiments, attributed to an orbital Rashba–Edelstein response.
AI.conclusion: The orbitronic response in MoTe₂ is governed by a thickness-driven structural phase transition, with the orbital Rashba–Edelstein effect identified as the dominant conversion mechanism in the metallic 1T′ phase.

title: Path-Measure Dynamics of Attention-Driven World Models: A Nonlocal Onsager--Machlup Approach
summary: Attention enables a world model to condition on its entire history, providing long-term memory that facilitates long-range predictions. While the local Onsager--Machlup theory in our companion paper assumes a temporally local predictive action, we investigate the conditions under which this locality holds. We derive the predictive path measure for latent dynamics that become non-Markovian due to attention-induced memory, demonstrating that this measure is the projection of a hidden linear Markov augmentation. Eliminating the auxiliary field results in a nonlocal Onsager--Machlup action, where memory manifests as a nonlocal quadratic form rather than a force. These kernels are completely monotone and exactly match a hidden Markov embedding with a finite relaxation spectrum; otherwise, the dynamics remain fundamentally nonlocal. By expanding the action in terms of the scale-separation parameter $ε=τ_{\text{mem}}/τ_{\text{dyn}}$, we show that the leading order recovers the local action of the companion paper, establishing locality as the short-memory limit of a nonlocal theory. We verify the reversible sector of this expansion term by term against an exactly solvable vector linear model.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates when predictive dynamics with attention-induced memory reduce to local (Markovian) behavior, showing that nonlocal memory effects emerge from a hidden Markov embedding and recover locality only in the short-memory limit.
AI.motivation: To understand the conditions under which the temporally local predictive action assumed in the companion paper's Onsager–Machlup theory holds, given that attention introduces non-Markovian long-term memory into the world model.
AI.method: Derives the predictive path measure for latent dynamics with attention-based memory; shows it is the projection of a hidden linear Markov augmentation; analyzes nonlocal Onsager–Machlup action; expands action via scale-separation parameter ε = τ_mem/τ_dyn; verifies against exactly solvable vector linear model.
AI.result: Memory appears as a completely monotone nonlocal quadratic form; dynamics remain fundamentally nonlocal unless a finite relaxation spectrum exists; the leading-order expansion recovers the local action from the companion paper, establishing locality as the short-memory limit.
AI.conclusion: Local predictive dynamics emerge only as an approximation when memory timescale is much shorter than dynamical timescale; otherwise the theory is inherently nonlocal.

title: Anisotropic tunneling through magnetic barriers in 8-Pmmn borophene
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures. Version to appear in Phys. Lett. A 2026
summary: We present a theoretical study of electron tunneling through a magnetic barrier in 8-Pmmn borophene, created by depositing two ferromagnetic strips on the borophene sheet. Using a low-energy effective Hamiltonian that captures the anisotropic Dirac spectrum, we solve the Dirac equation in three regions and impose wave-function continuity at the interfaces. From the resulting spinor solutions, we compute current densities and determine transmission and reflection probabilities as functions of incident energy, angle, and barrier parameters. The transmission exhibits strong anisotropy due to the tilted Dirac cones, with pronounced suppression for specific incident directions, suggesting directional filtering of carriers. We further calculate the conductance using the Landauer-Büttiker formalism, revealing that both magnetic strength and barrier width can tune the charge transport properties. The results demonstrate that engineered magnetic barriers in 8-Pmmn borophene enable precise control over electron flow, offering a platform for anisotropic transport control and tunable quantum devices. The interplay between the intrinsic anisotropy of borophene and external magnetic barriers provides rich opportunities to manipulate Dirac fermions in two-dimensional systems.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically investigates electron tunneling through magnetic barriers in 8-Pmmn borophene, showing anisotropic transmission due to tilted Dirac cones and demonstrating tunable charge transport via magnetic strength and barrier width, enabling directional filtering and quantum device applications.
AI.motivation: To understand how engineered magnetic barriers can control electron flow in anisotropic 8-Pmmn borophene, leveraging its unique tilted Dirac cone structure for directional transport manipulation.
AI.method: Using a low-energy effective Hamiltonian for the anisotropic Dirac spectrum, solving the Dirac equation in three regions with wave-function continuity, computing current densities and transmission/reflection probabilities, and calculating conductance via the Landauer-Büttiker formalism.
AI.result: Strong anisotropic transmission with pronounced suppression along specific incident directions, demonstrating directional filtering; tunable conductance controlled by magnetic barrier strength and width.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic barriers in 8-Pmmn borophene enable precise electron flow control, offering a platform for anisotropic transport control and tunable quantum devices, with rich opportunities to manipulate Dirac fermions via interplay of intrinsic anisotropy and external magnetic barriers.

title: Molecular interpretability of the bulk electrochemical impedance of concentrated electrolytes
comment: 13 manuscript pages with 6 figures; 2 pages methods and 1 figure; 100 references+footnotes; 8 pages appendices including 5 figures and a table
summary: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is a widely used technique to understand time-dependent response and relaxation under applied voltage. While these spectra contain a wealth of information, major gaps in our understanding can hinder our ability to interpret EIS spectra in terms of microscopic chemical mechanisms. We propose an alternative approach to common empirical fitting procedures for describing the contribution of the bulk electrolyte to the EIS spectrum. This new approach is rooted in determining the moments of the frequency-dependent conductivity, with molecular interpretability provided by a generalized Langevin equation description of an effective single particle dynamics; the `itinerant oscillator' (IO) model. In contrast to a Debye--Falkenhagen description, the IO model makes no assumptions regarding the concentration of the electrolyte, a fact we demonstrate by analysing molecular dynamics simulations of a room-temperature ionic liquid. By analysing the memory function from simulation within the framework provided by the IO model, we reveal the importance of capturing the separation of timescales within the memory function for describing the temperature dependent $β$-relaxation process. We go on to show how our impedance model directly reports on this distribution of timescales while retaining the simplicity of commonly employed workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an alternative to empirical fitting for interpreting electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) spectra of bulk electrolytes. The method uses moments of frequency-dependent conductivity and a generalized Langevin equation with the itinerant oscillator (IO) model. Unlike the Debye–Falkenhagen model, it works for any electrolyte concentration. Analysis of molecular dynamics simulations of a room-temperature ionic liquid shows the IO model captures the separation of timescales in the memory function, crucial for describing temperature-dependent β-relaxation, while maintaining workflow simplicity.
AI.motivation: Major gaps exist in interpreting EIS spectra in terms of microscopic chemical mechanisms; common empirical fitting procedures lack molecular interpretability, especially for concentrated electrolytes.
AI.method: The approach determines moments of frequency-dependent conductivity, grounded in a generalized Langevin equation description using the itinerant oscillator (IO) model. Memory functions from molecular dynamics simulations are analyzed within the IO framework.
AI.result: The IO model, unlike the Debye–Falkenhagen model, makes no assumptions about electrolyte concentration. It reveals that capturing the separation of timescales in the memory function is essential for describing the temperature-dependent β-relaxation process.
AI.conclusion: The impedance model directly reports on the distribution of timescales while retaining the simplicity of commonly used workflows, offering a physically interpretable alternative for EIS analysis.

title: Intrinsically low thermal conductivity of stoichiometric lithium niobate:Experimental measurement and microscopic origin
summary: With the rapid development of integrated electro-optic and nonlinear optical devices based on lithium niobate (LiNbO$_3$, LN), thermal management is becoming a critical area of focus. However, experimental measurement of thermal transport in stoichiometric LiNbO$_3$ (sLN) remains scarce, and the intrinsic microscopic mechanisms remain to be established. Here, we combine the laser pump-probe technique of frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) with state-of-the-art machine-learned atomistic simulations to comprehensively investigate thermal transport in sLN. The measured and simulated room-temperature thermal conductivity ($κ$) values of sLN agree well, which are orders-of-magnitude lower than that of many classic and emerging semiconductors such as silicon. Furthermore, the temperature-dependent $κ$ exhibits a $T^{-α}$ scaling with $α$ near unity, suggesting that thermal transport is dominated by intrinsic phonon-phonon scattering. By comparing sLN with cubic boron arsenide (cBAs) which serves as an ultrahigh-$κ$ benchmark, we reveal that harmonic properties are not responsible for the low $κ$ of sLN, which feature phonon heat capacity and group velocities that are either higher than or comparable to those in cBAs. Instead, the low $κ$ originates from substantially stronger anharmonicity and larger scattering phase space. These two factors collectively suppress phonon lifetimes by 1-2 orders of magnitude, leading to a maximum phonon mean free path of approximately 140 nm. As a result, notable size effects emerge in thin-film sLN below 1 $μ$m, with $κ$ dropping to half the bulk value at 10 nm. Altogether, our findings establish a fundamental understanding of thermal transport in sLN and provide atomistic insights for thermal management in advanced lithium niobate technologies.

AI.tldr: This paper combines FDTR experiments and machine-learned atomistic simulations to investigate thermal transport in stoichiometric LiNbO₃ (sLN). Room-temperature thermal conductivity is orders-of-magnitude lower than silicon, exhibits ~T⁻¹ scaling (intrinsic phonon-phonon scattering), and the low κ stems from strong anharmonicity and large scattering phase space (not harmonic properties).
