Maximum phonon mean free path ~140 nm, with size effects appearing below 1 μm.
AI.motivation: Thermal management is critical for rapidly developing integrated electro-optic and nonlinear optical devices based on lithium niobate, yet experimental thermal transport data for stoichiometric LiNbO₃ is scarce and the intrinsic microscopic mechanisms remain unclear.
AI.method: Combines frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) experiments with state-of-the-art machine-learned atomistic simulations to measure and compute thermal conductivity, temperature dependence, phonon properties, and scattering mechanisms in sLN.
AI.result: Room-temperature κ of sLN is orders-of-magnitude lower than silicon; temperature-dependent κ follows ~T⁻¹ scaling; low κ is not due to harmonic properties (heat capacity and group velocities are comparable to or higher than cBAs) but stems from strong anharmonicity and large scattering phase space, suppressing phonon lifetimes by 1-2 orders of magnitude; maximum phonon MFP ~140 nm; size effects reduce κ to half the bulk value at 10 nm thickness.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish a fundamental understanding of thermal transport in sLN and provide atomistic insights for thermal management in advanced lithium niobate technologies.

title: On the emergence of quantum many-body chaos for tunably-broken integrability
summary: We develop a quantitative theory for the emergence of quantum many-body chaos as integrability is broken via a tunable parameter. In a circuit model of free fermions, 'doped' with a tunable density of integrability-breaking gates, we uncover the microscopic mechanisms underpinning the crossover from early-time integrable behaviour to late-time chaos through the lens of the out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs). The integrability-breaking gates act as local, in spacetime, hotspots which locally amplify the OTOCs such that an accumulation of them eventually leads to fully-developed chaos. We identify the explicit characteristic time and length scales governing this crossover, as well as the dependence of the chaotic OTOC characteristics -- such as the butterfly velocity and front broadening -- on the integrability-breaking parameter.

AI.tldr: A quantitative theory for the emergence of many-body chaos as integrability is broken, using a fermionic circuit model doped with tunable integrability-breaking gates, revealing microscopic mechanisms of OTOC growth and identifying crossover time/length scales and chaotic characteristics.
AI.motivation: To quantitatively understand how quantum many-body chaos emerges when integrability is systematically broken, and to uncover the microscopic mechanisms underlying the crossover from integrable to chaotic behavior.
AI.method: A circuit model of free fermions doped with a tunable density of integrability-breaking gates; analysis of out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) to probe chaos.
AI.result: Identified explicit characteristic time and length scales governing the integrable-to-chaotic crossover; found that integrability-breaking gates act as local spacetime hotspots that locally amplify OTOCs; characterized dependence of butterfly velocity and front broadening on the integrability-breaking parameter.
AI.conclusion: Accumulation of local OTOC amplification from integrability-breaking hotspots leads to fully-developed chaos, with quantifiable crossover scales and chaotic OTOC features.

title: Theory of collective learning in populations of adaptive agents
summary:
We investigate homogeneous populations of smart active agents that exchange information with their neighbors to perform a decentralized learning process aimed at achieving a prescribed macroscopic state. Such agents may, for example, represent simple microrobots. The exchanged information comprises tunable parameters governing the agent dynamics, referred to as the individual policy, together with an internal memory encoding previously visited states. This memory is used to evaluate a reward that quantifies the success of a policy to achieve the prescribed state. We extend the kinetic-theory description of collective learning in spatially homogeneous systems [Phys. Rev. Lett. 134, 248302 (2025)] and derive formal evolution equations for the distribution of policies across the population. A central outcome of our theory is the emergence of an effective reward function that fully determines the evolution of the policy distribution and encapsulates the microscopic details of the agents physical and memory dynamics. We obtain closed equations for the policy mean and variance which admit explicit time-dependent solutions under the assumption of Gaussian-distributed memories and polices.
  To illustrate the framework, we present a series of minimal microscopic models, considering both perfect and partial separation of physical, memory and policy exchange time scales, as well as models with one- and two-dimensional policies. The obtained theoretical results compare well with agent-based numerical simulations. The theory captures key aspects of collective learning, including the influence of population diversity and reward fluctuations on learning performance. Finally, we discuss potential applications to swarm robotics and machine learning, and highlight connections with classical models of biological evolution, including the Replicator equation and the Moran model.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a kinetic theory of collective learning for smart active agents (e.g., microrobots) that exchange policies and memory to achieve a prescribed macroscopic state. It derives evolution equations for policy distributions, identifies an effective reward function, obtains closed-form solutions under Gaussian assumptions, and validates results with agent-based simulations, connecting to swarm robotics, machine learning, and biological evolution models.
AI.motivation: To theoretically understand and model how populations of homogeneous smart active agents (e.g., microrobots) can use decentralized exchange of policies and memory to collectively learn and achieve a desired macroscopic state.
AI.method: Extends kinetic-theory description of collective learning from spatially homogeneous systems; derives formal evolution equations for the distribution of policies; obtains closed equations for policy mean and variance under Gaussian-distributed memories and policies; validates with agent-based numerical simulations across minimal microscopic models with varied time-scale separations and policy dimensions.
AI.result: An effective reward function emerges that fully determines policy distribution evolution, encapsulating microscopic agent dynamics. Closed-form time-dependent solutions for policy mean and variance are obtained. Theory captures key collective learning aspects (population diversity, reward fluctuations) and compares well with simulations.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a unified theoretical foundation for collective learning in agent populations, with potential applications in swarm robotics and machine learning, and connections to classical biological evolution models (Replicator equation, Moran model).

title: Evidence for Deconfined Magnetic Order in the Kitaev-$J_3$ Model
summary: We investigate the Kitaev-$J_3$ honeycomb model using variational Monte Carlo calculations combined with a vison-quasiparticle analysis of the parent Kitaev spin liquid (KSL). We provide evidence for deconfined magnetic phases in which zigzag or antiferromagnetic order coexists with remnant $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological structure inherited from the KSL. The optimized variational wave functions retain multiple linearly independent topological sectors on a torus, whereas those of conventional ordered phases collapse to a single sector. The vison-quasiparticle analysis shows that magnetic order naturally arises from vison-pair condensation while single visons remain gapped, yielding a microscopic mechanism for magnetic ordering without immediate confinement. The resulting phases further host gapless spinons with multiple Majorana cones, offering a possible microscopic scenario for the anomalous low-temperature longitudinal thermal transport reported in magnetically ordered Kitaev materials such as Na$_2$Co$_2$TeO$_6$. Our results reveal a microscopic route to fractionalized magnetism beyond the conventional dichotomy between magnetic order and spin-liquid behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the Kitaev-$J_3$ honeycomb model and provides evidence for deconfined magnetic phases where zigzag or antiferromagnetic order coexists with $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological structure from the parent Kitaev spin liquid (KSL). Magnetic order arises from vison-pair condensation while single visons remain gapped, and the phases host gapless spinons with multiple Majorana cones, offering a microscopic scenario for anomalous thermal transport in materials like Na$_2$Co$_2$TeO$_6$.
AI.motivation: To understand whether magnetic order and spin-liquid behavior can coexist beyond the conventional dichotomy, and to explain anomalous low-temperature thermal transport observed in magnetically ordered Kitaev materials.
AI.method: Variational Monte Carlo calculations combined with vison-quasiparticle analysis of the parent Kitaev spin liquid.
AI.result: Optimized wave functions retain multiple linearly independent topological sectors on a torus; vison-pair condensation yields magnetic ordering without immediate confinement; the phases host gapless spinons with multiple Majorana cones.
AI.conclusion: There exists a microscopic route to fractionalized magnetism beyond the conventional dichotomy between magnetic order and spin-liquid behavior, with implications for understanding Kitaev materials like Na$_2$Co$_2$TeO$_6$.

title: The Wigner function for Integer quantum Hall effect
summary: Wigner's quasi-probability distribution function in phase space is a specialized representation of the density matrix, possessing significant physical importance. In this article, we first review the wave function describing electronic motion in an electromagnetic field under the Landau gauge. Next, based on an introduction to the properties of the Wigner function, we calculate the Wigner function for the integer quantum Hall effect using the integral method.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews electron wave functions in an electromagnetic field under Landau gauge, then calculates the Wigner function for the integer quantum Hall effect using integral methods.
AI.motivation: To connect Wigner's quasi-probability distribution function with the integer quantum Hall effect by calculating its explicit form for electrons in a Landau gauge electromagnetic field.
AI.method: The paper first reviews wave functions for electronic motion in an electromagnetic field under the Landau gauge, then introduces properties of the Wigner function, and finally uses an integral method to compute the Wigner function for the integer quantum Hall effect.
AI.result: A computed Wigner quasi-probability distribution function for the integer quantum Hall effect, derived via the integral method based on Landau gauge wave functions.
AI.conclusion: The Wigner function provides a phase-space representation of the integer quantum Hall effect, offering physical insights beyond the standard density matrix formulation.

title: Many-body benchmarking of DFT local-registry energetics in bilayer InSe
summary: Density functional theory (DFT) is widely used to model twisted bilayers, but the accuracy of the local stacking energetics underlying such models remains uncertain. Here, we benchmark the local-registry landscape of bilayer InSe using diffusion quantum Monte Carlo (DMC). DFT predicts that AB, AAr, and ABr stackings, which share the same interfacial Se registry, are nearly degenerate within 1.5 meV/f.u. and exhibit nearly indistinguishable DFT charge-density responses. DMC instead separates these stackings by 8(5) and 41(4) meV/f.u., while the energy difference between the most stable and least stable registries reaches 60(7) meV/f.u.. These large energy separations show that the stacking energetics are not determined by the interfacial atomic motif alone but depend on the full registry and its associated many-body electronic response. More broadly, these results show that DFT-based moiré models can substantially underestimate local stacking-energy corrugation, with direct consequences for predicted structural relaxation, domain formation, and electronic reconstruction in twisted layered materials.

AI.tldr: DFT significantly underestimates local stacking-energy corrugation in twisted bilayer InSe compared to DMC benchmarks, with energy differences up to 60(7) meV/f.u., revealing that stacking energetics depend on full registry and many-body electronic response, not just interfacial atomic motifs.
AI.motivation: To benchmark the accuracy of DFT-predicted local stacking energetics in twisted bilayers, which are widely used in moiré models but whose reliability remains uncertain.
AI.method: Benchmarked local-registry energetics of bilayer InSe by comparing DFT predictions with diffusion quantum Monte Carlo (DMC) calculations across different stacking configurations (AB, AAr, ABr).
AI.result: DFT predicts AB, AAr, and ABr stackings are nearly degenerate (within 1.5 meV/f.u.) with similar charge-density responses, but DMC separates these by 8(5) and 41(4) meV/f.u., with total energy corrugation up to 60(7) meV/f.u.
AI.conclusion: Stacking energetics depend on full registry and many-body electronic response, not just interfacial atomic motifs; DFT-based moiré models can substantially underestimate stacking-energy corrugation, affecting predictions of structural relaxation, domain formation, and electronic reconstruction in twisted layered materials.

title: Exact amplitude relations for diffusion-limited aggregation
summary: It has been known for several decades that the third moment of the multifractal spectrum of the harmonic measure for diffusion-limited aggregates is linked to the underlying fractal dimension of the cluster. We demonstrate, using an argument based on the Hastings-Levitov formulation of diffusion-limited aggregation (DLA) in two dimensions, an even stronger link, connecting the universal amplitude of the third moment to the cluster fractal dimension. This argument can be used for both the standard circular DLA as well as DLA in a cylinder (i.e., with periodic boundary conditions).

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a universal link between the amplitude of the third moment of the harmonic measure multifractal spectrum and the fractal dimension of DLA clusters in two dimensions, using the Hastings-Levitov framework for both circular and cylindrical geometries.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate a stronger universal relationship between the third moment of the harmonic measure multifractal spectrum and the fractal dimension of DLA clusters, beyond the previously known link.
AI.method: The argument is based on the Hastings-Levitov formulation of diffusion-limited aggregation in two dimensions, applied to both standard circular DLA and cylindrical DLA (with periodic boundary conditions).
AI.result: The universal amplitude of the third moment of the harmonic measure multifractal spectrum is directly connected to the cluster fractal dimension in DLA.
AI.conclusion: There exists a stronger, universal link between the third moment amplitude and fractal dimension in DLA, valid for both circular and cylindrical geometries.

title: Plaid-Like Spin Splitting and Chirality of Magnon Bands in Antiferromagnetic MnTe$_2$
summary: Altermagnets constitute an emerging class of magnetic materials that combine compensated antiferromagnetic order with spin-split excitations arising from crystalline symmetries. Despite strong theoretical interest, their experimental identification remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate that helicity- and angle-resolved Raman scattering measurements reveal reduced rotational symmetries of magnons and a pronounced imbalance between left- and right-circular polarization channels, indicating momentum-dependent magnon handedness. First-principles DFT+$U$ calculations combined with linear spin-wave theory uncover a characteristic plaid-like spin-splitting structure in momentum space. The resulting magnon spin textures are dictated by the unconventional sublattice symmetries of MnTe$_2$ and closely emulate those of altermagnetic electronic bands. Our work provides evidence of chiral spin-wave excitations unique to this non-coplanar antiferromagnet.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that helicity- and angle-resolved Raman scattering reveals reduced rotational symmetries of magnons and chiral spin-wave excitations in MnTe₂, identifying it as an altermagnet with plaid-like magnon spin textures confirmed by DFT+U calculations.
AI.motivation: Altermagnets are theoretically predicted but experimentally challenging to identify; the authors aim to provide unambiguous experimental evidence of altermagnetic behavior through magnon spectroscopy.
AI.method: Helicity- and angle-resolved Raman scattering measurements combined with first-principles DFT+U calculations and linear spin-wave theory.
AI.result: Observation of reduced rotational symmetries of magnons, imbalance between left- and right-circular polarization channels indicating momentum-dependent magnon handedness, and a plaid-like spin-splitting structure in momentum space.
AI.conclusion: MnTe₂ exhibits chiral spin-wave excitations unique to non-coplanar antiferromagnets, with magnon spin textures closely emulating altermagnetic electronic bands, confirming its altermagnetic nature.

title: Quantum-geometric shift of quasiequilibrium: Origin of nonreciprocal current driven by quantum-metric dipole
summary: We study nonlinear DC electric transport of quantum-metric origin by combining adiabatic perturbation theory with the nonequilibrium Green function approach. The adiabatic ansatz provides a basis for directly treating a DC electric field in the velocity gauge, rather than introducing it as the zero-frequency limit of an AC field. The resulting adiabatic-basis Hamiltonian takes the same form as in the length gauge, enabling a systematic comparison across different formulations. Applying this fully quantum formulation, we find a longitudinal nonreciprocal current governed by the quantum-metric dipole. The essential ingredient is a quantum correction to the distribution function that is absent in semiclassical treatments. We trace this correction to the finite spread of an electron wave packet during relaxation under a bias field, thereby identifying shifted quasiequilibrium as the physical origin of quantum-metric nonreciprocal transport.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a fully quantum formulation of nonlinear DC transport arising from quantum geometry, combining adiabatic perturbation theory with nonequilibrium Green functions. It reveals that a longitudinal nonreciprocal current is governed by the quantum-metric dipole, originating from a quantum correction to the distribution function—identified as shifted quasiequilibrium due to the finite spread of electron wave packets under bias.
AI.motivation: To develop a consistent quantum-mechanical framework for studying nonlinear DC electric transport of quantum-metric origin, addressing limitations of semiclassical treatments and clarifying the physical origin of quantum-metric nonreciprocal transport.
AI.method: Combines adiabatic perturbation theory with the nonequilibrium Green function approach; treats DC electric field directly in the velocity gauge via the adiabatic ansatz, and reformulates the Hamiltonian to match the length-gauge form for cross-framework comparison.
AI.result: Identifies a longitudinal nonreciprocal current governed by the quantum-metric dipole, arising from a quantum correction to the distribution function that is absent in semiclassical treatments.
AI.conclusion: The quantum correction originates from shifted quasiequilibrium—the finite spatial spread of an electron wave packet during relaxation under bias—establishing this as the physical origin of quantum-metric nonreciprocal transport.

title: Alternative routes to universal diversity scaling in component systems: from proteomes to large language models
summary: Remarkably common statistical laws characterize the diversity scaling and its fluctuations across a wide range of complex "component systems". These regularities are often interpreted as signatures of an underlying innovation mechanism driving the growth of component diversity, but the basic ingredients necessary for their emergence remain poorly understood. In particular, from language and technological artifacts to genomes and gene expression patterns, the number of distinct components grows sublinearly with system size, while its variance scales approximately as the square of its mean. This behavior is consistent across diverse systems, raising the question of whether general constraints or emergent principles underlying diversity and innovation define the architectures of realizations with different numbers of components. To address this question, we derive analytical conditions for the joint emergence of these two diversity laws within a broad class of growth models, showing that they require a specific asymptotic dependence of the innovation probability on diversity and system size. We then demonstrate that the same macroscopic laws arise in a different class of models with latent heterogeneity, where quadratic fluctuation scaling always emerges asymptotically as a consequence of general statistical principles, essentially the law of total variance, without explicitly assuming an innovation mechanism or any specific rule for system assembly. We compare these predictions with empirical data from language, genomes, LEGO constructions, and texts generated by large language models. Our results show that empirical diversity scaling laws strongly constrain generative models but do not uniquely identify the mechanisms generating diversity, revealing a close correspondence between innovation-driven growth models and latent-variable descriptions.

AI.tldr: The paper explores why diverse systems (languages, genomes, LEGO, LLM texts) show universal statistical laws: sublinear growth of distinct components with system size and quadratic scaling of variance with mean. The authors derive conditions for these laws in innovation-driven growth models and show they also emerge from latent heterogeneity models via the law of total variance. Empirical tests reveal that these laws constrain generative models but do not uniquely identify the underlying mechanisms.
AI.motivation: To understand whether general constraints or emergent principles underlie universal diversity scaling laws observed across complex component systems, and to determine if these laws uniquely identify the generative mechanisms.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of conditions for diversity scaling laws in a broad class of growth models, plus comparison with a latent heterogeneity model class. Empirical validation using data from languages, genomes, LEGO constructions, and large language model texts.
AI.result: Two key diversity laws (sublinear component growth, quadratic variance scaling) require specific asymptotic dependence of innovation probability on diversity and system size in growth models, but emerge generically in latent heterogeneity models via the law of total variance. Empirical data matches both classes, showing the laws constrain but do not uniquely identify mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Diversity scaling laws strongly constrain generative models but are insufficient to uniquely identify the mechanisms generating diversity; innovation-driven growth and latent-variable descriptions are closely related and can produce the same macroscopic patterns.

title: Unconventional Mixed-Parity Magnetism in Rare-Earth Tetraborides
comment: Main manuscript: 10 pages, 4 figures, Supplementary Material: 12 pages, 11 figures, 1 table
summary: Altermagnetism has advanced the study of compensated magnets by revealing non-relativistic spin splitting, traditionally classified into strictly even- or odd-parity spin textures. Here, we unveil a fundamentally different regime: component-resolved mixed-parity spin splitting in a fully three-dimensional compensated magnet. Using first-principles calculations, tight-binding and $\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{p}$ models, along with spin-group symmetry analysis, we demonstrate that the non-coplanar ground state of $\mathrm{TbB}_4$ enforces a unique momentum-space spin texture. The in-plane spin components exhibit odd-parity $p$- and $f$-wave-like textures, whereas the out-of-plane component retains an even-parity $d$-wave altermagnetic character. Crucially, the coexistence of the in-plane odd-parity textures is driven not by relativistic spin-orbit coupling, but by a staggered Berry phase arising from the inherent scalar spin chirality. This mixed-parity structure dictates distinct transport fingerprints, including bulk non-relativistic Edelstein and spin Hall responses, as well as a symmetry-allowed Berry curvature dipole. These results establish the rare-earth tetraborides as a robust platform for engineering complex spin-charge conversion phenomena.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals component-resolved mixed-parity spin splitting in the 3D compensated magnet TbB₄, where in-plane spin components show odd-parity textures while out-of-plane component retains even-parity altermagnetic character, driven by staggered Berry phase from scalar spin chirality rather than spin-orbit coupling, leading to distinct transport responses.
AI.motivation: To go beyond traditional classification of altermagnetic spin textures (strictly even or odd parity) and explore a fundamentally different regime of mixed-parity spin splitting in fully three-dimensional compensated magnets.
AI.method: First-principles calculations, tight-binding and k·p models, and spin-group symmetry analysis.
AI.result: In TbB₄, in-plane spin components exhibit odd-parity p- and f-wave-like textures, while out-of-plane component retains even-parity d-wave altermagnetic character; the odd-parity textures arise from staggered Berry phase from scalar spin chirality, not spin-orbit coupling.
AI.conclusion: The mixed-parity structure enables bulk non-relativistic Edelstein and spin Hall responses, and a symmetry-allowed Berry curvature dipole; rare-earth tetraborides serve as a robust platform for engineering complex spin-charge conversion phenomena.

title: Density functional study of native point defects in CaO
summary: We investigate the structural, electronic, and optical properties of native point defects in CaO using first-principles density-functional calculations. Oxygen vacancies are favored under O-poor conditions, whereas calcium vacancies dominate under O-rich conditions. Calculated migration barriers and binding energies indicate that vacancy complexes are thermodynamically stable and can survive high-temperature annealing. Optical transition energies, evaluated using the Franck-Condon framework, suggest that several experimentally observed absorption and emission peaks can be attributed to negatively charged vacancy complexes as well as isolated oxygen vacancies.

AI.tldr: This paper uses DFT calculations to study native point defects in CaO, finding oxygen vacancies favored under O-poor conditions and calcium vacancies under O-rich conditions. Vacancy complexes are thermodynamically stable and survive high-temperature annealing, and optical transitions from negatively charged vacancy complexes and isolated oxygen vacancies match experimental absorption/emission peaks.
AI.motivation: To understand the structural, electronic, and optical properties of native point defects in CaO, which are critical for its performance in applications such as catalysis, optoelectronics, and as a refractory material.
AI.method: First-principles density-functional theory (DFT) calculations combined with the Franck-Condon framework for optical transition energies.
AI.result: Oxygen vacancies dominate under O-poor conditions; calcium vacancies dominate under O-rich conditions. Vacancy complexes are thermodynamically stable and survive high-temperature annealing. Negatively charged vacancy complexes and isolated oxygen vacancies correspond to experimentally observed absorption and emission peaks.
AI.conclusion: The identified defect configurations and their optical signatures provide a microscopic assignment for experimental optical spectra in CaO, linking specific vacancy types and complexes to observed absorption/emission features.

title: How wrong is too wrong: A numerical study on the relevance of positional memory in the generalized Langevin equation
summary: If a generalized Langevin equation contains a potential of mean force, it cannot at the same time contain a linear memory kernel and a fluctuating force that obeys a second fluctuation dissipation theorem in the sense of Kubo, and be exact. As modelers often prefer to use generalized Langevin equations that have the first three properties, one needs to ask how close the model dynamics is to the dynamics of the underlying microscopic system. To test this, we analyze a simple model system in which the potential of mean force can be well approximated by a polynomial of low order. The exact generalized Langevin equation of this model contains memory terms in addition to the linear one. We show that these additional terms, at least for the model system regarded in this article, are important for the dynamics and cannot be neglected if one intends to model core aspects of the underlying system correctly.

AI.tldr: Generalized Langevin Equations (GLEs) combining a potential of mean force, linear memory kernel, and Kubo's second fluctuation-dissipation theorem cannot be exact; additional nonlinear memory terms are dynamically significant and cannot be neglected for accurate modeling.
AI.motivation: To test how closely the commonly used GLE model (with potential of mean force, linear memory, and second FDT) approximates the true microscopic dynamics, given that it cannot be exact.
AI.method: Analyze a simple model system where the potential of mean force is approximated by a low-order polynomial; derive the exact GLE and compare it to the simplified GLE that omits nonlinear memory terms.
AI.result: The exact GLE contains additional (nonlinear) memory terms beyond the linear memory kernel; these terms are dynamically important and cannot be neglected.
AI.conclusion: Simplified GLEs with only linear memory fail to capture core aspects of the underlying dynamics; the extra memory terms are essential for correct modeling.

title: Phonon spectral function of Holstein polaron: Investigation of many-body effects with self-energy and vertex correction
summary: We study the impact of the many-body effects on the phonon spectral function of Holstein polaron in one-dimension in the antiadiabatic regime by incorporating the contributions from the electron self-energy and vertex corrections within a weak-coupling approach that respects the charge-conserving Ward identity. We find that while the polaronic spectral weight is suppressed due to contribution from the electron self-energy, on the other hand, the same is enhanced due to contribution from the vertex corrections. While strength of both the contributions increases with increasing the wave vector ($\q$) of phonons, they nearly cancel each other for the small-$\q$ modes so that the polaronic spectral weight is weakly affected due to the many-body effects. For the large-$\q$ modes near the zone boundary, the net many-body correction is dominated by the contribution of the electron self-energy which increases faster in comparison to that of the vertex corrections with increasing the wave vector thereby resulting in a significant suppression of the polaronic spectral weight. We find that while the weak-coupling perturbative approach provides a reliable estimation of the impact of the many-body effects deep inside the antiadibatic regime, the renormalization of quasiparticle spectrum must be taken into account for an accurate estimation when the phonon energy approaches the electronic bandwidth.

AI.tldr: The paper studies many-body effects on the Holstein polaron phonon spectral function in 1D antiadiabatic regime using a charge-conserving weak-coupling approach. Electron self-energy suppresses polaronic spectral weight while vertex corrections enhance it; they nearly cancel for small-q modes, but self-energy dominates for large-q modes near the zone boundary, causing significant suppression. Perturbation works deep in antiadiabatic regime, but quasiparticle renormalization is needed when phonon energy approaches electronic bandwidth.
AI.motivation: To understand the impact of many-body effects (electron self-energy and vertex corrections) on the phonon spectral function of the Holstein polaron in one dimension, particularly in the antiadiabatic regime, using a charge-conserving approach.
AI.method: Weak-coupling perturbative approach incorporating both electron self-energy and vertex corrections, respecting the charge-conserving Ward identity, applied to the 1D Holstein model in the antiadiabatic regime.
AI.result: Electron self-energy suppresses and vertex corrections enhance polaronic spectral weight. For small-q modes, contributions nearly cancel; for large-q modes near zone boundary, self-energy dominates, causing significant suppression. Perturbation is reliable deep in antiadiabatic regime but requires quasiparticle renormalization when phonon energy approaches bandwidth.
AI.conclusion: Many-body effects significantly affect the Holstein polaron phonon spectral function depending on phonon wave vector. A charge-conserving treatment is essential. Weak-coupling perturbation is valid deep in antiadiabatic regime, but quasiparticle spectrum renormalization is required for accurate results near the bandwidth limit.

title: Quantifying angular momentum of coherently driven circular phonons
summary: The use of intense terahertz (THz) pulses to manipulate low-energy excitations offers a powerful approach for ultrafast control of electronic and magnetic properties in materials. Theory suggests that circular ionic motions driven by THz fields carry angular momentum, potentially generating internal magnetic fields. Recent experiments in nonmagnetic SrTiO3 (STO) have hinted at such THz-induced fields, but their origin remains debated. Here, we employ ultrafast x-ray diffraction to resolve the time-dependent ionic trajectories in STO following excitation by circularly polarized THz pulses. Our analysis reveals that oxygen ions, despite their lower mass, contribute around 90% of the phonon angular momentum. The resulting imbalance between the negatively and positively charged ions provides a clear explanation for the mechanism behind induced magnetism in STO. This work further provides the first quantitative measurement of circular ionic motions and their angular momentum and establishes a general methodology for the investigation of angular momentum transfer in solids, paving the way for new strategies to control topological phonon transport and phonon-driven magnetism in quantum materials.

AI.tldr: Using ultrafast x-ray diffraction, the authors resolve THz-driven ionic trajectories in SrTiO3, finding that oxygen ions contribute ~90% of phonon angular momentum, explaining the mechanism of THz-induced magnetism in nonmagnetic SrTiO3.
AI.motivation: To resolve the debated origin of THz-induced internal magnetic fields in nonmagnetic SrTiO3 by directly measuring circular ionic motions and their angular momentum.
AI.method: Ultrafast x-ray diffraction to resolve time-dependent ionic trajectories in SrTiO3 excited by circularly polarized THz pulses.
AI.result: Oxygen ions contribute ~90% of the phonon angular momentum; the charge imbalance between negatively and positively charged ions explains the induced magnetism.
AI.conclusion: Provides the first quantitative measurement of circular ionic motions and angular momentum, establishing a general methodology for studying angular momentum transfer in solids and enabling control of phonon-driven magnetism and topological phonon transport in quantum materials.

title: Velocity and force autocorrelations in Brownian dynamics with a Lorentz force
summary:
We derive a general relation between the velocity and force autocorrelation tensors (VACT and FACT) for a Brownian particle subject to an external magnetic field. Using time-symmetry arguments, we show that, for the full Langevin dynamics, the VACT depends only on the FACT, independently of the details of the interaction potential. Under the hypothesis of timescale separation between thermalization and interaction-driven motion, this relation simplifies considerably in the overdamped (Brownian) limit. A central feature of the overdamped result is that, unlike in the field-free case, the part of the VACT that controls the self-diffusion of the particle couples to the antisymmetric part of the FACT, with a coupling strength set by the ratio of the cyclotron frequency to the thermalization rate. We validate and illustrate the formalism on an exactly solvable model: a dimer of charged particles bound by a harmonic potential. Depending on the relative sign of the particle charges, the magnetic field is found to produce either a transient suppression of mobility and diffusion that is fully recovered at long times, or a persistent oscillatory force autocorrelation, regions of negative mobility, and a
  long-time suppression of self-diffusion.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a general relation between velocity and force autocorrelation tensors (VACT and FACT) for a Brownian particle in a magnetic field, showing that VACT depends only on FACT regardless of interaction potential. In the overdamped limit, the self-diffusion-controlling part of VACT couples to the antisymmetric part of FACT, with coupling strength determined by the ratio of cyclotron frequency to thermalization rate. The formalism is validated on a model of a charged dimer in a harmonic potential, revealing either transient suppression of diffusion or persistent oscillations, negative mobility, and long-time diffusion suppression depending on charge sign.
AI.motivation: To derive a general, potential-independent relation between velocity and force autocorrelation tensors for Brownian particles in a magnetic field, and to understand how the magnetic field modifies self-diffusion and mobility beyond the field-free case.
AI.method: Time-symmetry arguments applied to full Langevin dynamics, followed by timescale separation to obtain the overdamped (Brownian) limit. The formalism is validated on an exactly solvable model: a harmonically bound dimer of charged particles.
AI.result: In the overdamped limit, the VACT controlling self-diffusion couples to the antisymmetric part of the FACT, with coupling strength given by the cyclotron frequency to thermalization rate ratio. For the charged dimer model, depending on charge sign, the magnetic field causes either (1) transient suppression of mobility and diffusion fully recovered at long times, or (2) persistent oscillatory force autocorrelation, negative mobility regions, and long-time suppression of self-diffusion.
AI.conclusion: The derived relation is general and independent of interaction potential details. The magnetic field introduces qualitatively different diffusive behaviors depending on the sign of particle charges, including regimes of negative mobility and long-term diffusion suppression.

title: A density matrix renormalization group approach to quantum point contacts
summary: Using the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) combined with the correction-vector method, we investigate the competition between an harmonic potential and repulsive interactions in a one-dimensional fermionic system. The parabolic confinement induces spatial inhomogeneity, and by tuning its curvature one can continuously interpolate between a potential well--relevant for cold-atom setups--and a quantum barrier, as realized in mesoscopic systems such as quantum point contacts. We analyze how the ground-state particle distribution evolves with the strength and sign of the confining potential and how the confinement reshapes the spectral weight of the local density of states (LDOS) at the center of the chain. In the barrier regime, a localized peak emerges in the electron part of the spectrum ($ω>0$) as a direct consequence of the potential. In contrast, in the well configuration and for weak interactions, a localized feature persists but shifts to the hole sector ($ω<0$). However, for stronger interactions, the LDOS no longer displays clear signatures of the external potential, indicating that correlations dominate over single-particle confinement.

AI.tldr: Using DMRG and correction-vector method, this paper studies a 1D fermionic system under competing harmonic confinement and repulsive interactions, showing how the ground-state density and local density of states evolve across potential well to barrier regimes, with interaction strength determining whether confinement or correlations dominate.
AI.motivation: To understand the competition between harmonic confinement and repulsive interactions in 1D fermionic systems, and how tuning the curvature of a parabolic potential from a well (cold-atom setups) to a barrier (quantum point contacts) reshapes particle distribution and spectral properties.
AI.method: Density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) combined with the correction-vector method.
AI.result: In the barrier regime, a localized peak emerges in the electron part (ω>0); in the well with weak interactions, a localized feature appears in the hole sector (ω<0); for stronger interactions, LDOS shows no clear signatures of the external potential, indicating correlation dominance.
AI.conclusion: The interplay between confinement strength and interaction strength determines the spectral features; correlations can wash out single-particle confinement signatures in the LDOS.

title: Entropy of Non-Abelian Anyons from Slow Quasiparticle Dynamics in Quantum Hall Interferometers
summary: Non-Abelian anyons emerging in fractional quantum Hall states carry a characteristic entropy, $ΔS = k_B \log d$, where \(d\) is the anyon's quantum dimension. This \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) entropy can, in principle, be extracted from charge measurements of an antidot via Maxwell relations. However, equilibrium charge measurements in fractional antidots have proven to be challenging with conventional charge detectors. Here, we propose a scheme based on an antidot embedded in an interferometer, in which the charge can be inferred from the recently observed time-dependent switching of the interference phase. Performing such non-local charge measurements at equilibrium, the characteristic \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) entropy of non-Abelian anyons (e.g., $d = \sqrt{2}$ for the $ν= 5/2$ state) can be extracted for intermediate temperatures, which exceed the level spacing of the interferometer edge, but are much smaller than the level spacing of the antidot.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scheme to measure the 𝒪(1) entropy of non-Abelian anyons (e.g., d=√2 at ν=5/2) by embedding an antidot in an interferometer and inferring charge from time-dependent phase switching, enabling extraction of the characteristic entropy at intermediate temperatures.
AI.motivation: Non-Abelian anyons in fractional quantum Hall states carry characteristic entropy ΔS = k_B log d, but equilibrium charge measurements in fractional antidots with conventional charge detectors have been challenging.
AI.method: The scheme embeds an antidot in an interferometer, inferring charge from time-dependent switching of the interference phase, enabling non-local charge measurements at equilibrium.
AI.result: The characteristic 𝒪(1) entropy of non-Abelian anyons can be extracted for intermediate temperatures that exceed the level spacing of the interferometer edge but are much smaller than the antidot level spacing.
AI.conclusion: Non-local charge measurements via interferometric phase switching provide a viable route to measure the entropy signature of non-Abelian anyons, overcoming limitations of conventional charge detectors.

title: HVAF Spraying of NiTi Coatings: Microstructure, Phase Transformation and Shape Memory Behavior
summary: Depositing various coatings on surface of engineering components with the aim to improve their performance concerning wear, corrosion, friction and thermal protection is already a standard practice. Depositing metallic NiTi shape memory alloy coatings may be a viable alternative for hard ceramic coatings. NiTi coatings offer additional benefits originating from unique functional thermomechanical properties. However, fabrication of thick NiTi coatings turned out to be difficult. Standard electroplating and laser cladding methods are not suitable for NiTi the most widely used plasma spray methods tend to produce chemically inhomogeneous coatings that do not transform martensitically, cold sprayed NiTi coatings suffer from poor adhesion to the substrates. In this work we report on first ever successful fabrication of thick NiTi coatings (100-300 um) that display functional thermomechanical properties and simultaneously show very good adherence to the substrate. We used high velocity air fuel thermal spray method to fabricate NiTi coatings deposited on mild steel using four different sets of processing parameters. Chemical composition, porosity, microstructure, phase transformation and functional thermomechanical properties of the NiTi coatings were evaluated. Although the coatings contain inhomogeneous microstructure, voids, oxide particles, high density of dislocation defects and internal stress, they undergo martensitic transformation upon cooling and or mechanical loading. As sprayed NiTi coatings need to be annealed to display functional thermomechanical properties. Despite their limited tensile strength, the coatings displayed thermal actuation in 3 point bending tests and shape memory effects in nanoindentation and scratch tests.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first successful fabrication of thick NiTi shape memory alloy coatings (100-300 μm) on mild steel using high velocity air fuel (HVAF) thermal spray, which exhibit martensitic transformation, good adhesion, thermal actuation, and shape memory effects despite microstructural imperfections.
AI.motivation: To overcome existing difficulties in fabricating thick NiTi coatings that display functional thermomechanical properties and good substrate adhesion, as standard methods (electroplating, laser cladding, plasma spray, cold spray) each suffer from specific drawbacks such as chemical inhomogeneity, poor adhesion, or inability to produce thick coatings.
AI.method: High velocity air fuel (HVAF) thermal spray method with four different processing parameter sets; post-deposition annealing; characterization via chemical composition, porosity, microstructure, phase transformation analysis, and functional testing (3-point bending, nanoindentation, scratch tests).
AI.result: Coatings exhibited inhomogeneous microstructure with voids, oxides, dislocations, and internal stress, but still underwent martensitic transformation upon cooling/mechanical loading; after annealing, they displayed thermal actuation in 3-point bending and shape memory effects in nanoindentation and scratch tests, though tensile strength was limited.
AI.conclusion: HVAF thermal spray combined with post-deposition annealing is a viable method for producing thick NiTi coatings with functional thermomechanical properties and good adhesion, offering an alternative to hard ceramic coatings for wear, corrosion, friction, and thermal protection applications.

title: Contrarian Majority Dynamics: Violation of Detailed Balance and Nonequilibrium Steady States
summary: I revisit the Galam Majority Model (GMM) with contrarian agents from a statistical-mechanics perspective, revealing three fundamental features. First, in addition to the GMM simultaneous-update of small discussion groups, I construct a related single-agent stochastic dynamics, providing a Markovian microscopic representation, which is found to yield the same evolution equation. Second, I show that, contrary to what is often stated in the literature, the GMM closed evolution equation for the opinion density is not the result of a mean-field approximation. Indeed, I derive the conventional mean-field dynamics associated with majority-rule interactions and show that it yields a distinct, probabilistic evolution equation contrary the deterministic GMM equation. I therefore identify the GMM as an iterated mean-field dynamics. Third, I investigate the thermodynamic nature of the dynamics obtained from both single-agent and simultaneous updates. Both are shown to violate detailed balance. However, while Kolmogorov's cycle condition is satisfied for single-agent updates, it is violated for simultaneous updates, making the departure from equilibrium stronger in the latter case. I then compute the probability flux in the stationary state and show that it is non-vanishing, confirming the absence of an effective Hamiltonian and establishing that the stationary state is a genuine nonequilibrium steady state.These results clarify the statistical-mechanical foundations of the GMM and establish contrarian majority dynamics as an intrinsically non-equilibrium process with distinct regimes of irreversibility. Contrarians are not thermal noise.

AI.tldr: The paper reexamines the Galam Majority Model with contrarian agents, showing it is not a mean-field approximation, constructing a Markovian single-agent dynamics, and establishing the model as an iterated mean-field dynamics with genuine nonequilibrium steady states violating detailed balance, where contrarians act as non-thermal sources of irreversibility.
AI.motivation: To clarify the statistical-mechanical foundations of the Galam Majority Model (GMM) with contrarian agents and resolve misconceptions in the literature regarding its mean-field nature and equilibrium properties.
AI.method: The author constructs a single-agent stochastic Markovian dynamics counterpart to the simultaneous-update GMM, derives the conventional mean-field dynamics for majority-rule interactions, analyzes detailed balance and Kolmogorov's cycle condition for both update schemes, and computes the probability flux in the stationary state.
AI.result: (1) The single-agent dynamics yields the same evolution equation as the simultaneous-update GMM. (2) The GMM equation is not a mean-field approximation but an iterated mean-field dynamics, distinct from the probabilistic conventional mean-field dynamics. (3) Both update schemes violate detailed balance; single-agent updates satisfy Kolmogorov's cycle condition while simultaneous updates do not; the stationary state has non-vanishing probability flux, confirming a genuine nonequilibrium steady state.
AI.conclusion: Contrarian majority dynamics is intrinsically a nonequilibrium process with distinct irreversibility regimes; contrarians act as a source of irreversibility distinct from thermal noise, and the GMM is fundamentally different from equilibrium statistical-mechanical models.

title: Fundamental limitations of single-particle Green's-function zeroes as probes of many-body topology
summary: We show that topological invariants constructed from single-particle Green's functions (GFs) cannot reliably diagnose the topology of interacting many-body states. Using coupled interacting SSH chains as a minimal example, we demonstrate that a spin-spin interaction can trivialize the many-body ground state without affecting the GF topological invariant. This breakdown originates from the GF's inability to probe electronic excitations in the Fock sectors responsible for the topological degeneracy. Consequently, GF zeroes are not associated with physical topological quasiparticles and cannot generally characterize interacting topological phases.

AI.tldr: Topological invariants from single-particle Green's functions fail to reliably diagnose interacting many-body topology, as shown via coupled SSH chains where spin-spin interaction trivializes the ground state without changing the GF invariant, because GFs cannot probe Fock sectors underlying topological degeneracy.
AI.motivation: To test whether single-particle Green's function topological invariants can reliably diagnose the topology of interacting many-body states.
AI.method: Using coupled interacting SSH chains as a minimal example, the authors examine the effect of spin-spin interaction on the many-body ground state and compare it with single-particle GF topological invariants.
AI.result: Spin-spin interaction can trivialize the many-body ground state without affecting the GF topological invariant. GF zeroes are not associated with physical topological quasiparticles.
AI.conclusion: Single-particle Green's function topological invariants cannot generally characterize interacting topological phases due to their inability to probe Fock sectors responsible for topological degeneracy.

title: Josephson and Spin Currents in Coupled Polariton Condensates
summary: We analyze particle and spin currents in networks of coupled spinor exciton-polariton condensates arranged as plaquettes and regular polygonal rings. In closed geometries, spin-conserving and TE-TM-induced spin-flip tunnelling combine to generate circulating particle currents, hidden spin counterflows, and bond-dependent spin-current patterns. For the minimal geometries - an equilateral triangle, and a square plaquette - we derive analytical expressions for edge-resolved currents from stationary configurations obtained by energy minimization. We then show how particle, in-plane spin, and out-of-plane spin currents partition the parameter plane and provide direct signatures of the equilibrium phases. Finally, we apply the same current-resolved diagnostics to larger rings, where winding numbers and a branch-invariant common-phase coherence metric organize the resulting phase structure.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes particle and spin currents in networks of coupled spinor exciton-polariton condensates arranged as plaquettes and polygonal rings, deriving analytical expressions for edge-resolved currents from stationary configurations and showing how different current types partition the parameter plane, with applications to larger rings using winding numbers and a common-phase coherence metric.
AI.motivation: To understand how spin-conserving and TE-TM-induced spin-flip tunneling generate circulating particle currents, hidden spin counterflows, and bond-dependent spin-current patterns in coupled spinor exciton-polariton condensate networks.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of edge-resolved currents from stationary configurations obtained by energy minimization for minimal geometries (equilateral triangle and square plaquette), extended to larger polygonal rings with winding numbers and a branch-invariant common-phase coherence metric.
AI.result: Identification of how particle, in-plane spin, and out-of-plane spin currents partition the parameter plane and provide direct signatures of equilibrium phases; organization of phase structure in larger rings via winding numbers and common-phase coherence metric.
AI.conclusion: Current-resolved diagnostics effectively characterize equilibrium phases in closed geometries of coupled spinor polariton condensates, revealing rich current patterns including hidden spin counterflows.

title: Transition-Metal Tailored $Ga_{2}O_{2}$ Monolayer: From Room-Temperature Gas Sensing to Chemical Scavenging
summary: Pristine $Ga_{2}O_{2}$ monolayers suffer from poor sensitivity and weak molecular capture, limiting their application in toxic gas detection and environmental detoxification. Here, we employ first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate the gas sensing and scavenging properties of $Ga_{2}O_{2}$ monolayers substitutionally tailored via seven transition-metals (TM): Pd, Zn, Zr, Mo, Ag, Ti, and Pt. All TM-substituted monolayers exhibit negative formation and binding energies, negligible lattice distortion, and structural stability in molecular dynamics simulations. Performance evaluation against eight toxic industrial and three environmental gases reveals functionalities ranging from selective, reusable room-temperature sensing to permanent molecular capture. Ag substitution exhibits exceptional selectivity for $NO$ with moderate adsorption strength (~-0.83eV), an up to eight-order-of-magnitude conductivity enhancement, besides facilitating reusable $O_2$ and $NO_2$ detection. Additionally, Pd-, Zn-, Zr-, and Mo substitutions tune selectivity toward $NO$, $NO_2$, $CO_2$, $CO$, and $O_2$. Coming to applications towards toxic gas capture, Zr- and Mo-substituted systems selectively scavenge oxidizing gases, whereas Ti and Pt act as universal scavengers. Further analysis reveals that Pd- and Ag-substituted monolayers remain selective for $NO$, while Zn substitution favors $NO_2$ detection even in ambient atmospheric conditions. Thus, these tailored $Ga_{2}O_{2}$ monolayers offer a practical platform for atmospheric monitoring and detoxification.

AI.tldr: TM-substituted Ga₂O₂ monolayers are investigated via DFT for gas sensing and scavenging. Ag shows exceptional NO selectivity with high conductivity enhancement; Pd, Zn, Zr, Mo tune selectivity toward various gases; Ti and Pt act as universal scavengers, offering a platform for atmospheric monitoring and detoxification.
AI.motivation: Pristine Ga₂O₂ monolayers suffer from poor sensitivity and weak molecular capture, limiting their use in toxic gas detection and environmental detoxification.
AI.method: First-principles DFT calculations to investigate gas sensing and scavenging properties of Ga₂O₂ monolayers substitutionally doped with seven transition metals (Pd, Zn, Zr, Mo, Ag, Ti, Pt).
AI.result: Ag substitution shows exceptional NO selectivity (~-0.83 eV adsorption), eight-order-of-magnitude conductivity enhancement, and reusable O₂/NO₂ detection. Pd, Zn, Zr, Mo tune selectivity toward NO, NO₂, CO₂, CO, O₂. Zr/Mo selectively scavenge oxidizing gases; Ti/Pt act as universal scavengers. Pd/Ag remain selective for NO; Zn favors NO₂ detection even in ambient conditions.
AI.conclusion: TM-tailored Ga₂O₂ monolayers provide a practical platform for atmospheric monitoring and detoxification.

title: Correlation and entanglement dynamics of free fermions in disguise
summary: We study the nonequilibrium dynamics following a quantum quench in spin chains that can be solved via a mapping to free fermions in disguise. These models feature an exponential degeneracy of all energy eigenvalues, raising the question of the validity of the established framework describing the properties of integrable systems out of equilibrium. We present two main results. First, we develop an analytic method to compute the quasi-momentum distribution function characterizing the generalized Gibbs ensemble, and derive an analytic formula to compute the corresponding expectation values for special observables. Second, we conjecture a modification of the standard formula for the entanglement growth based on the quasi-particle picture, taking into account that each fermion in disguise carries an additional amount of entropy due to the exponential degeneracy of the energy eigenvalues. We test our theoretical predictions against numerical tensor-network computations for different initial states and Hamiltonian parameters. For the local observables, we find excellent agreement. For the entanglement dynamics, we find small deviations suggesting that our conjecture is only approximately correct. Our results represent a first step towards the extension of the established framework of integrable systems out of equilibrium to models hosting free fermions in disguise.

AI.tldr: This paper studies nonequilibrium dynamics after quantum quenches in spin chains that map to free fermions in disguise. The authors develop an analytic method to compute the quasi-momentum distribution for the generalized Gibbs ensemble and propose a modified formula for entanglement growth accounting for exponential eigenvalue degeneracy. They test predictions against tensor-network numerics, finding excellent agreement for local observables and small deviations for entanglement dynamics.
AI.motivation: The exponential degeneracy of all energy eigenvalues in these models challenges the validity of the standard framework describing integrable systems out of equilibrium, motivating the need for a new theoretical approach.
AI.method: Analytic method to compute the quasi-momentum distribution function for the generalized Gibbs ensemble; a conjectured modification of the standard quasi-particle picture for entanglement growth accounting for additional entropy from exponential degeneracy; numerical tensor-network computations for validation.
AI.result: Excellent agreement with numerics for local observables; small deviations for entanglement dynamics, indicating the conjecture is only approximately correct.
AI.conclusion: The results represent a first step towards extending the established framework of integrable systems out of equilibrium to models hosting free fermions in disguise.

title: Anomalous thermopower from the drag of overdamped collective modes
summary: Inspired by the observation of a Seebeck coefficient ratio that exhibits a seemingly logarithmic divergence at low temperature in high-temperature superconducting cuprates, we show that a mechanisms similar to the standard phonon drag can give rise to anomalies in the thermopower of a metal, if the dragged collective mode is overdamped, with a damping coefficient that increases with lowering the temperature. Our finding adds a piece to the puzzle of the strange-metal behavior observed in many different systems and supports our proposal that overdamped charge density fluctuations can be responsible of such a behavior in high-temperature superconducting cuprates.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that an overdamped collective mode (analogous to phonon drag but with damping increasing at low temperatures) can explain the logarithmic divergence in the Seebeck coefficient ratio observed in high-temperature superconducting cuprates, supporting the role of overdamped charge density fluctuations in strange-metal behavior.
AI.motivation: To explain the anomalous logarithmic divergence of the Seebeck coefficient ratio observed at low temperatures in high-temperature superconducting cuprates, which is part of the broader strange-metal behavior puzzle.
AI.method: The authors extend the standard phonon drag mechanism to a scenario where the dragged collective mode is overdamped, with a damping coefficient that increases as temperature decreases.
AI.result: The overdamped collective mode drag mechanism produces anomalies in the thermopower that resemble the experimentally observed logarithmic divergence in the Seebeck coefficient ratio.
AI.conclusion: This mechanism adds to the understanding of strange-metal behavior and supports the proposal that overdamped charge density fluctuations are responsible for such behavior in high-temperature superconducting cuprates.

title: Coupled Spin-Orbital $p$-Wave Magnetism via Structural and Magnetic Chirality
summary: Helical spin textures represent the minimal realization of $p$-wave magnetism which is characterized by momentum-odd spin polarization. Independently, structurally chiral crystals exhibit momentum-odd orbital polarization arising from broken inversion symmetry. Here, we demonstrate that spin-orbit coupling couples these two independent microscopic chirality degrees of freedom, allowing the orbital polarization of a chiral crystal to generate an additional contribution to the $p$-wave spin splitting. The resulting spin-orbital state is naturally classified by the relative chirality $η=χ_{\mathrm c}χ_{\mathrm m}$, giving rise to two symmetry-distinct $p$-wave phases corresponding to homochiral and heterochiral configurations which can be directly probed by the longitudinal conductivity. These phases exhibit distinct transport signatures, establishing relative chirality as an experimentally accessible symmetry degree of freedom in chiral magnetic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that in chiral crystals, spin-orbit coupling links structural chirality (orbital polarization) and magnetic chirality (spin polarization), creating two distinct p-wave phases defined by relative chirality (homochiral vs heterochiral), which can be distinguished via longitudinal conductivity measurements.
AI.motivation: To understand how spin-orbit coupling couples the two independent microscopic chirality degrees of freedom (structural vs magnetic) in chiral crystals, and to classify the resulting spin-orbital states by their relative chirality.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis demonstrating that spin-orbit coupling in structurally chiral crystals allows orbital polarization to contribute to p-wave spin splitting, with the resulting states classified by the relative chirality parameter η = χ_c χ_m.
AI.result: Two symmetry-distinct p-wave phases emerge: homochiral and heterochiral configurations, which exhibit distinct transport signatures in longitudinal conductivity.
AI.conclusion: Relative chirality is established as an experimentally accessible symmetry degree of freedom in chiral magnetic systems, directly probed by longitudinal conductivity measurements.

title: A depth resolved investigation of hydrogen uptake in carbon based nanostructures by soft-to-hard photoemission spectroscopy
summary: Hydrogen chemisorption on graphitic carbon modifies the carbon orbital hybridization from sp2 to sp3, altering both structural and electronic properties. Understanding not only the lateral extent but also the depth distribution of hydrogen uptake in three-dimensional carbon architectures is essential for both fundamental studies and storage applications. To this end, we investigate here the evolution of the C 1s core-level lineshape in nanoporous graphene (NPG) and vertically aligned carbon nanotubes (CNTs) upon hydrogenation, exploiting soft-to-hard X-ray photoemission spectroscopy to achieve a depth-resolved analysis. Decomposition of the C 1s spectra reveals the formation of an sp3 rich overlayer in both systems, with an effective thickness ranging from a fraction of a graphitic monolayer (NPG) to approximately one graphitic layer (CNTs), indicating limited hydrogen penetration beneath the outermost accessible surfaces. Overall, hydrogenation in both materials remains predominantly localized on the surface. These results clarify the spatial distribution of hydrogen in curved and porous graphitic networks and provide quantitative constraints on its chemisorption for carbon-based hydrogen storage applications.

AI.tldr: Hydrogen chemisorption on nanoporous graphene and vertically aligned carbon nanotubes primarily occurs on the surface, forming an sp³-rich overlayer with limited penetration, as revealed by depth-resolved X-ray photoemission spectroscopy.
AI.motivation: To understand the lateral extent and depth distribution of hydrogen uptake in three-dimensional carbon architectures, which is essential for both fundamental studies and hydrogen storage applications.
AI.method: Depth-resolved analysis using soft-to-hard X-ray photoemission spectroscopy to study the evolution of C 1s core-level lineshapes in nanoporous graphene (NPG) and vertically aligned carbon nanotubes (CNTs) upon hydrogenation.
AI.result: Decomposition of C 1s spectra shows an sp³-rich overlayer with effective thickness ranging from a fraction of a graphitic monolayer (NPG) to ~1 graphitic layer (CNTs), indicating limited hydrogen penetration beneath the outermost surfaces.
AI.conclusion: Hydrogenation in curved and porous graphitic networks is predominantly surface-localized, providing quantitative constraints on hydrogen chemisorption for carbon-based hydrogen storage.

title: A Fuzzy Sphere Journey in Critical Phenomena
comment: Invited review. Submitted May 2025; revised September 2025; published March 2026
summary: This review discusses the recently proposed fuzzy sphere regularization for studying $2+1$D critical phenomena, particularly three-dimensional (3D) conformal field theory (CFT). The fuzzy sphere scheme not only offers remarkable efficiency in extracting extensive CFT data at low computational cost but also reveals unexpected connections among 3D CFT (critical phenomena), noncommutative geometry, and the quantum Hall effect. We introduce the fundamental ideas of fuzzy sphere regularization, emphasizing its role in demonstrating the state-operator correspondence of 3D CFTs on the $S^2 \times \mathbb{R}$ geometry. Additionally, we review key developments in this approach across various directions and outline potential future applications.

AI.tldr: This review introduces fuzzy sphere regularization as an efficient computational method for studying 3D conformal field theory and critical phenomena, revealing connections between noncommutative geometry and the quantum Hall effect.
AI.motivation: To provide an efficient computational approach for extracting conformal field theory data in 2+1D critical phenomena, and to uncover unexpected theoretical connections between 3D CFT, noncommutative geometry, and the quantum Hall effect.
AI.method: Fuzzy sphere regularization, which maps 3D CFTs onto the S² × ℝ geometry using noncommutative geometry techniques, leveraging the state-operator correspondence.
AI.result: The fuzzy sphere scheme achieves remarkable efficiency in extracting extensive CFT data at low computational cost and reveals unexpected connections among 3D CFT, noncommutative geometry, and the quantum Hall effect.
AI.conclusion: The fuzzy sphere regularization is a powerful and efficient tool for studying 3D CFTs and critical phenomena, with promising future applications across multiple directions.

title: Intrinsic orbital Hall effect in a nonuniform electric field
summary: Geometric analysis of electronic Bloch states offers a universal framework for understanding electronic properties, yet its role in the transport of orbital angular momentum remains unexplored. In this work, we establish an analytic connection between orbital angular momentum transport and the geometric properties of Bloch wave functions in electronic systems. Focusing on the intrinsic orbital Hall effect in the dc limit under a spatially nonuniform electric field, we show that its conductivity can be expressed in terms of universal geometric quantities, such as the orbital Berry curvature and quantum metric. This formulation provides a term-by-term correspondence with the geometric description of intrinsic charge Hall transport established in previous studies. Using a tight-binding model, we further illustrate that the higher-order orbital Hall response can exhibit enhanced sensitivity to the orientation of an anisotropic sample. Our work deepens the understanding of diverse intrinsic transverse transport phenomena and the role of quantum geometry in electronic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes an analytic connection between orbital angular momentum transport and geometric properties of Bloch wave functions, showing that intrinsic orbital Hall conductivity can be expressed via orbital Berry curvature and quantum metric, with a term-by-term correspondence to intrinsic charge Hall transport.
AI.motivation: While geometric analysis of Bloch states is well-established for understanding electronic properties, its role in orbital angular momentum transport was previously unexplored. The authors aim to bridge this gap.
AI.method: Analytic derivation connecting orbital angular momentum transport to geometric properties (orbital Berry curvature and quantum metric) of Bloch wave functions, focusing on the intrinsic orbital Hall effect in the dc limit under spatially nonuniform electric fields. A tight-binding model is used for illustration.
AI.result: The intrinsic orbital Hall conductivity can be expressed in terms of universal geometric quantities with a term-by-term correspondence to the geometric description of intrinsic charge Hall transport. Higher-order orbital Hall response shows enhanced sensitivity to sample orientation in anisotropic systems.
AI.conclusion: This work deepens the understanding of diverse intrinsic transverse transport phenomena and the role of quantum geometry in electronic systems.

title: Anisotropic nanoscale coherent polariton transport in CrSBr
summary: In a combined experimental and theoretical study, we demonstrate anisotropic polariton transport on the nanoscale in the van der Waals antiferromagnet CrSBr. While effective cavity-polariton formation emerges via the self-hybridization of ultra-high oscillator strength excitons with a thin slab photonic mode, the absence of external mirrors facilitates spectroscopic investigation of these polaritons via cathodoluminescence (CL) on length scales determined by the electron wavelength. This direct access allows us to perform precise charting of the polariton landscape with nanometric resolution, and to probe polariton interference phenomena. The main finding of the work highlights that the coherent polariton transport follows the $C_{2v}$ symmetry of CrSBr, allowing exclusive transport along the crystallographic a-axis, while no coherent feature is found along the b-axis direction. Our work sets the foundation to use CL spectroscopy in cavity-polaritonics in more advanced landscapes, such as photonic crystals or optical lattices, and establishes the technique as a powerful tool to probe anisotropic expansion and relaxation phenomena on the nanoscale

AI.tldr: This study demonstrates anisotropic nanoscale polariton transport in the van der Waals antiferromagnet CrSBr using cathodoluminescence spectroscopy, showing coherent transport exclusively along the crystallographic a-axis following C2v symmetry.
AI.motivation: To investigate anisotropic polariton transport on the nanoscale in a van der Waals antiferromagnet without external mirrors, using cathodoluminescence for direct nanometric-resolution probing of polariton behavior in cavity-polaritonics.
AI.method: Combined experimental and theoretical study using self-hybridized cavity-polaritons formed from ultra-high oscillator strength excitons and thin slab photonic modes in CrSBr, probed via cathodoluminescence spectroscopy with nanometric spatial resolution.
AI.result: Coherent polariton transport follows C2v symmetry of CrSBr, enabling exclusive transport along the crystallographic a-axis with no coherent features observed along the b-axis direction.
AI.conclusion: CL spectroscopy is established as a powerful tool for cavity-polaritonics, capable of probing anisotropic expansion and relaxation phenomena on the nanoscale, with potential applications in photonic crystals and optical lattices.

title: Coherent two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy integrated with confocal back focal plane microscopy
summary: We introduce a setup for coherent two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy in the pump-probe reflection geometry that is integrated with a confocal back focal plane imaging microscope. The angle-resolved capability is utilized to control pump and probe wavevectors, while real space imaging enables co-localization of the collection spots for linear and ultrafast experiments. Compression of pulses down to 20 fs is achieved. We demonstrate the capabilities of this approach on an exfoliated WSe$_2$ monolayer on Si/SiO$_2$. The setup is suited to investigate excitons and exciton-polaritons in 2D Materials and their heterostructures.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a novel setup for coherent 2D electronic spectroscopy in reflection geometry, integrated with confocal microscopy, enabling angle-resolved and real-space imaging capabilities for studying excitons and exciton-polaritons in 2D materials, demonstrated on a WSe₂ monolayer.
AI.motivation: To develop a spectroscopic technique that combines coherent two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy with angle-resolved and real-space imaging capabilities, specifically suited for investigating excitons and exciton-polaritons in 2D materials and their heterostructures.
AI.method: Integration of coherent 2D electronic spectroscopy in pump-probe reflection geometry with a confocal back focal plane imaging microscope, utilizing angle-resolved capability to control pump and probe wavevectors, real-space imaging for co-localization, and pulse compression down to 20 fs.
AI.result: Successful demonstration of the setup on an exfoliated WSe₂ monolayer on Si/SiO₂, showing the capability to perform ultrafast spectroscopy with angle-resolved wavevector control and real-space co-localization.
AI.conclusion: The setup is well-suited for investigating excitons and exciton-polaritons in 2D materials and their heterostructures, enabling both linear and ultrafast experiments with high spatial and angular resolution.

title: From Bloch to Néel: Anisotropy-dependent Domain-Wall Character in FePd Thin Films
summary: We report an experimental investigation of the depth-dependent domain wall formation in L1$_0$-FePd thin films with high perpendicular magnetic anisotropy. Using circular dichroism X-ray resonant magnetic scattering (CD-XRMS) as a function of the incident X-ray angle, we explore the depth evolution of chiral spin textures in two samples with different strengths of magnetocrystalline anisotropy. Combined with CD-STXM, CD-ptychography, and macroscopic characterization of the structural order, magnetic properties, and surface morphology, we relate these observations to differences in the long-range order of the L1$_0$ phase of FePd. One FePd thin film with very high magnetocrystalline anisotropy, characterized by $Q_{PMA}=1.8$, exhibits an unexpectedly large Néel contribution. Angular-dependent CD-XRMS directly reveals a smooth transition from a hybrid Bloch-Néel chirality within the upper FePd layer towards a purely Néel-type structure at the lower FePd interface. In the second FePd sample, despite a still relatively large $Q_{PMA}=1.45$, the domain walls were found to be purely Néel type. These results indicate a crucial role of the long-range structural order in determining the formation of the magnetic structure.

AI.tldr: Using CD-XRMS as a function of incident X-ray angle, the study reveals depth-dependent domain wall chirality transitions in L1₀-FePd thin films, showing that samples with very high magnetocrystalline anisotropy (Qₚₘₐ=1.8) exhibit a hybrid Bloch-Néel to pure Néel transition from upper to lower interface, while samples with slightly lower anisotropy (Qₚₘₐ=1.45) show purely Néel walls, highlighting the critical role of long-range structural order in magnetic structure formation.
AI.motivation: To investigate the depth-dependent evolution of chiral spin textures in L1₀-FePd thin films with high perpendicular magnetic anisotropy, and to understand how variations in magnetocrystalline anisotropy and long-range structural order influence domain wall chirality transitions.
AI.method: Circular dichroism X-ray resonant magnetic scattering (CD-XRMS) at varying incident X-ray angles, combined with CD-STXM, CD-ptychography, and macroscopic characterization of structural order, magnetic properties, and surface morphology.
